#3198. watchOS 27.3: Three new features coming soon to Apple Watch

watchOS 27.3 will launch to all users next month and introduce these three new Apple Watch features.

Siri AI keeps getting new features and also expanding to more languages. And in watchOS 27.3, the assistant will improve in both categories.

watchOS 27.3 upgrades Siri AI with new app actions across built-in apps like Calendar, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, and Weather. With these capabilities, Siri on your wrist can do more than ever.

There are also four new Siri AI languages supported in watchOS 27.3: Chinese (traditional), Norwegian, Turkish, and Vietnamese.

For the latest Apple Watch models, watchOS 27.3 adds a new Audio Intelligence feature called Live Rewind. Per Apple’s website:

Live Rewind recalls what was just said in the last 15 seconds by showing a text snippet on your Apple Watch when you double-press the Digital Crown, so you can catch something you missed or are less familiar with. You can ask Siri about the content of the snippet or simply save it to the Siri app.

I’m curious to see how useful this proves in everyday life. When Apple demoed the feature in September, it showed Live Rewind being used at a restaurant when an Apple Watch user missed part of the server’s menu explanation. Asking the server to repeat what they said seems like an easier solution, but perhaps there are other occasions Live Rewind will come in handy.

It won’t be for everyone, but I’ve been testing watchOS 27.3’s new Siri Recap feature and really love it.

Siri Recap only works on Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, and it’s off by default. But if you have one of those models and enable the feature, Siri can create automatic logs of what’s happening in your day-to-day life.

Most of the time, you won’t need to reference any of the recaps and they’ll be automatically deleted after a week. But based on my experience with the feature, Siri Recap definitely comes in handy at times when trying to remember key details from conversations.

Which of watchOS 27.3’s new features are you most interested in? Let us know in the comments.

#3196. SpaceX aborts Starship booster catch, but the ship is still in orbit

The booster diverted into the Gulf after detecting a fault. Ship 42 tries the first upper-stage catch on Saturday.

SpaceX launched Starship on its 15th test flight on Friday, but called off its first attempt to catch both stages of the rocket. The Super Heavy booster aborted its return to the launch tower and came down in the Gulf of Mexico instead.

The upper stage, Ship 42, reached orbit and released 26 Starlink satellites, Spaceflight Now reported. It is due to fly back to Starbase in Texas on Saturday, where SpaceX will try to catch it with the tower’s mechanical arms for the first time.

The rocket lifted off from Starbase at 4:47pm local time on Friday. The booster was meant to return to the pad about six minutes later.

Instead, the booster cancelled the catch on its own after detecting a guidance and navigation problem, SpaceX commentator Dan Huot said on the company’s webcast. It switched to a backup landing offshore, and exploded just before hitting the water, according to Spaceflight Now.

SpaceX has caught a Super Heavy booster three times before. However, it has never caught the newer, larger version 3 booster, or the upper stage.

It was the second time Starship has reached orbit. On its first orbital flight in September, an engine failure forced SpaceX to bring the ship down early.

This time, the ship is due to spend about 22 hours in orbit and circle the Earth about 14 times, UPI reported. SpaceX can still end the flight early and send it into the ocean if problems arise.

Catching the upper stage would be a key step towards a fully reusable rocket, which SpaceX says it needs to cut launch costs and fly to the Moon and Mars.

#3195. 1 ETF That Can Turn $500 Monthly Into a $600,000 Portfolio That Pays Out $18,000 Annually

Consistency can go a long way with this ETF.

Ask almost anyone how an extra $1,500 a month sounds, and I'm sure they'll say it sounds great. Ask them how it would sound to have it come in with no extra work, and I'm sure they'll tell you it sounds really great.

Getting to $1,500 in monthly dividends won't happen overnight for most investors, but history shows that consistently investing in the Schwab U.S. Dividend Equity ETF (SCHD +0.53%) can put you well on your way.

At its historical growth rate, $500 invested monthly into SCHD could grow into a $600,000 portfolio that pays out $4,500 a quarter, or $1,500 a month. Let’s take a look at how.

Since it began trading in October 2011, SCHD has averaged a 13.7% annual total return (including dividends). If it sustains that average, $500 monthly investments could reach $600,000 in about 21 years. Realistically, that could be tough to maintain, so we'll use a more modest 10.2%, its annual average excluding dividends.

With those returns, $500 monthly investments could grow to $600,000 in 25 years. And aside from having $600,000 to your name, one of the best parts is that you would've invested only $150,000 over that time, highlighting the power of compound earnings.

Right now, SCHD's dividend yield is 2.9%, but its average over the past decade has been around 3.2%. If we meet in the middle and assume a 3% yield, $600,000 invested in SCHD would pay out $18,000 annually ($4,500 quarterly).

Past results don't guarantee future performance, so we shouldn't assume SCHD will continue at its historical rate. However, its structure gives me confidence in its ability to sustain growth.

Many ETFs focus mainly on grouping stocks with high dividend yields. Yes, the higher the yield, the higher the payout, but not all high-yield stocks are worth holding. Plenty of stocks have high yields because their stock price has struggled due to poor business performance.

SCHD helps investors avoid those situations by focusing more on business quality and financial health. To be considered, a company must check all of the following boxes:

Most companies that check those boxes are mature and reliable, so you shouldn't have to worry about one-hit wonders or sudden dividend cuts.

Most of SCHD's holdings come from the consumer staples, healthcare, and energy sectors, which checks out, given how cash-generative they tend to be. Its top 10 holdings are:

SCHD isn't weighted by market cap like most indexes and popular ETFs; it uses a modified method. This is how you get companies like Texas Instruments ahead of Procter & Gamble and Home Depot ahead of Coca-Cola. Holding weights aside, of SCHD's 102 holdings, 11 are Dividend Kings (companies with at least 50 consecutive years of increases):

Having nearly 11% of its holdings in Dividend Kings is a testament to SCHD's commitment to holding shareholder-friendly companies that have stood the test of time.

One of the best things you can do is take advantage of your brokerage platform’s dividend reinvestment plan (DRIP). When you enroll in a DRIP, your platform takes the dividends you're paid and automatically reinvests them in the stock or ETF that paid them instead of paying you out in cash.

Using a DRIP compounds the effect because the dividends you reinvest start earning dividends themselves and become shares that can appreciate over time. That's typically a better route than receiving relatively small cash payouts and will speed up the process of reaching the $600,000 mark.

Denzel and Davis both throw heat in 'Fences'

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Verdict: This period drama is a well-executed adaptation of August Wilson's award-winning 1985 play of the same name. Unfortunately, it notably feels like you're watching a play; it struggles to make the case for why it's a dramatic work of cinema as opposed to a theatrical revival. But as Denzel Washington and Viola Davis start pitching a perfect game, you stop nitpicking and let the performances take over.

Where to watch: Stream "Fences" for free on Tubi or YouTube

"Fences" was a movie I circled on my calendar as I made my way through this year-long Denzel Watchathon. This is considered a seminal work in the legendary actor's career. It's his third directorial effort in his filmography and by far the best. It also earned him his seventh Oscar nomination as an actor (his second of three he'd earn in the 2010s alone).

Once you watch it, it's no surprise why this performance makes the highlight reel. This movie is essentially crafted to serve his character, except for the few scenes where it's designed to highlight Viola Davis. She plays Denzel's on-screen wife in this period drama film, and I'd argue it's her performance that's the more impressive of the two.

Unfortunately, if I have to nitpick, this strength is also the movie's biggest weakness. "Fences" is adapted from August Wilson's 1985 play of the same name. That play was a roaring success, earning Wilson both a Pulitzer and a Tony Award in 1987. Watching this film adaptation, one wouldn't be shocked if Denzel and Wilson (who also wrote the screenplay for this movie) didn't change a thing from the Broadway version. The entire time, it feels unmistakably like you're watching a play.

This isn't inherently a bad thing; I often like movies adapted from plays, and to be clear, I thought this film was excellent. But unlike, say, "A Few Good Men," I failed to see what was added to the performances, to the story, etc., by turning Wilson's play into a cinematic experience. If you had simply had this same cast act out the play on a stage and filmed it on a Sony Handycam, it'd probably be just as good.

If you want to watch this movie before you read on, I have good news! It's currently streaming for free on Tubi, one of the best free streaming services we've tested. You can also stream it for free on YouTube (with ads).

Here are some of the other Denzel Washington movies I've covered to date in my Denzel Watchathon:

Read more: Every Denzel Watchathon movie so far

The sixth installment in August Wilson's 10-part "Pittsburgh Cycle," "Fences," centers around Troy. Portrayed by Denzel Washington in this adaptation, he's a middle-aged man working as a sanitation worker. He appears to be an ordinary working-class Pittsburgher, albeit sans Yinzer accent. But as the story unfolds, it's quickly apparent that Troy wasn't always destined for an ordinary life.

Troy, as revealed by his longtime friend, Bono (Stephen McKinley Henderson), was at one point one of the best baseball players in America. But he had the bad luck of being a Black player in the years before Jackie Robinson broke the color barrier in Major League Baseball. So while his Negro League career earned him plaudits and adulation, it didn't exactly bring in the cash. And you can only dine on praise for so long before reality sets in.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Complicating things is ... well, everything else. His marriage to Rose (Viola Davis) appears healthy, but early on in the movie there are hints this isn't the case. It's clear that money can be a pain point for Troy, who now has less of it than ever because he's no longer collecting part of his brother's (Mykelti Williamson) disability check from the Army. When Troy's 34-year-old son, Lyons (Russell Hornsby), comes asking for money, it's clear that Troy thinks he'll never see that money again, and that he doesn't have enough cash to waste. Even on family.

But it's not Lyons's relationship with his father at the core of "Fences." Instead, the film focuses on Troy's relationship with his other son, Cory. He's 17 years old and the only child produced by Troy and Rose's marriage. His relationship with his dad is somewhat rocky and complicated by the fact that colleges are recruiting Cory for football. Troy, a former pro athlete who now makes a living hauling trash, wants Cory to avoid sports entirely for fear that it will lead him down the same path Troy went down.

Davis is more subtle in her performance. She's not given a ton to do at first, but then she's given some devastating news in a later scene, and it allows her to steal the scene. From that moment on, she steals the entire movie.

Despite all this focus on Troy and his sons, it's Viola Davis who steals the movie as Rose. Denzel is supposed to be excellent in this movie. He's given incredible lines. He's the main character. Every character exists in this story to be a reflection of his impact on their lives or to highlight a trial and tribulation Troy has had to deal with. There's a scene early on where Cory asks why Troy doesn't like him, and Denzel just cooks, as the Gen Z youths would say. In fact, if you've seen a scene from this movie on TikTok, it's probably this scene of Denzel as Troy taking his son down a peg.

Davis is more subtle in her performance. She's not given a ton to do at first, but then she's given some devastating news in a later scene, and it allows her to steal the scene. From that moment on, she steals the entire movie.

In that aforementioned scene, she's not openly weeping, sobbing, or screaming at the top of her lungs, all of which would be perfectly reasonable responses given the news she just received. However, she manages to do a feat of physical acting where snot just runs from her nostrils. It's the clear aftermath of a moment of grief, underlying the fact that she's not nearly as composed as she's forcing herself to appear on the outside.

When I say that Davis steals this movie and doesn't let go, I mean it. She was the lone Oscar winner for "Fences," deservedly taking home the Oscar for Best Supporting Actress. It might be the first movie since "The Manchurian Candidate" where I felt that an actress took the spotlight from Denzel and there was simply nothing he could do about it.

But again, Denzel is great in this movie. He earns an Oscar nomination; the movie itself earns a Best Picture nomination, in no small part due to his performance and direction. It's a tough watch at times. Because it feels like a play but lacks the intimate, almost physical connection between thespian and theatergoer, it can also lose your interest on occasion.

That all is quickly brushed aside, though, as the film reaches its climax. The performances at the center of this movie are the definition of must-watch. And now that it's currently available to stream at home for free, you really have no excuse not to check it out if you haven't already.

#3193. Apple offers a military discount, here’s how to get it

If you’re a member of the U.S. military, Apple offers an easy way to save 10% on eligible products and accessories. It’s available to current and veteran members of the U.S. military and their immediate family members living in the same household. While you’ll need to verify your eligibility to access the discount, the process is simple. There are also a few limitations you’ll want to know about before placing an order. Here’s everything you need to know.

A 10% discount is available to current and Veteran members of the US Military, National Guard and Reserve. Immediate family members who reside in the same household are also eligible.

Verification is handled through ID.me. Creating an ID.me account is free, and current military members can verify their service using their .mil email address. Veterans can enter details of their service information for ID.me to verify, or upload images of official documents (such as a DD-214) for ID.me to review and confirm their eligibility. Once you’re verified, your ID.me account can also be used to access military discounts from other retailers and services that support ID.me verification.

Once verified, you can start shopping by visiting Apple’s Store for Veterans and Military. The discount only applies to Apple products and accessories (including Beats) so third-party products aren’t eligible. Apple services, such as Apple Music and iCloud+, are also excluded. Orders can be shipped directly to you, or you can choose in-store pickup if the product is available at a nearby Apple Store.

This is probably the biggest catch. Apple specifically says ACMI isn’t available when shopping through the Veterans and Military Store. You can still earn 3% back in Daily Cash with Apple Card, but you lose the option to finance your purchase at 0% interest over several months. Apple Upgrade also isn’t available when purchasing through the military store.

The only way to get the military discount is to make your purchase through Apple’s website in a browser. The Apple Store app isn’t an option, which means you also can’t take advantage of Apple’s “Get Ready” feature to select your iPhone model, color, storage capacity, and carrier ahead of pre-orders opening. Instead, you’ll have to navigate Apple’s website on launch day, when demand is high and server traffic can make checkout more challenging. Whether the 10% savings is worth giving up the convenience of a potentially quicker checkout is ultimately up to you.

The military discount can’t be combined with carrier promotions or discounts on iPhone purchases. You can still trade in your existing iPhone through Apple and receive the applicable trade-in value, but you can’t take advantage of carrier-specific trade-in offers, like promotions that give you a larger credit when you trade in an eligible device and activate or upgrade a line.

These purchase limits reset on January 1 each year.

Apple’s military discount is a useful perk, especially if you’re buying a product at launch and want to save 10% right away. However, it’s worth comparing prices with other retailers before you buy, since sales and promotions can sometimes beat Apple’s discount. The military store also comes with a few limitations, so you’ll want to weigh the savings against the features and payment options you’re giving up. Even with those caveats, 10% off can make a real difference on an expensive Apple purchase.

#3191. Microsoft restores Outlook and Teams after two-day global outage

Microsoft outage disrupts Outlook, Teams and Copilot worldwide, with Claude and ChatGPT integrations also affected

Microsoft logo at the Microsoft Experience Center, New York

Microsoft said on Saturday that it had restored service to its remaining customers and regions, about two days after the outage began, the Associated Press reported.

The company said the problem was caused by an issue during an earlier upgrade to its network capacity, which surfaced after a recent network change. It again said there was no sign of malicious activity, and said on Friday that the outage was not caused by AI agents.

Separately, US officials said the outage was not linked to Friday’s nationwide flight ground stop.

A global Microsoft outage has disrupted Outlook, Teams, Copilot and other Microsoft 365 services for more than 12 hours, affecting businesses, government agencies, financial institutions and airlines across several continents.

The disruption has also spread to third-party AI services, with OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude reporting problems with their Microsoft 365 connectors.

The trouble began on Thursday in the Americas and spread globally within an hour. Outage reports reached 74 countries and territories in that time, according to Downdetector, which recorded a tenfold jump in UK reports at 17:43 UTC, followed by surges in India and New Zealand as their workdays began.

Microsoft has ruled out a cyberattack. Charles Lamanna, the company’s executive vice president for Copilot, Agents and Platform, said on X that there was no indication the disruption resulted from malicious or cyber activity.

@MSFT365Status We regret that today’s outages caused disruptions for our customers, and we are working to address the issue. We will continue to share more information as soon as we have it, and for now I can confirm that there is no indication this is the result of malicious or cyber activity.

— Charles Lamanna (@clamanna) November 13, 2026

However, restoring services has proved more difficult than initially expected. After reporting positive results from its recovery measures, Microsoft said overnight that traffic rerouting and strategic blocking were delivering only partial improvements, rather than sustained recovery.

The company has continued restarting affected servers and applying additional mitigation measures, but some changes have not worked as expected.

The outage has had consequences well beyond Microsoft’s own products. Bankers at Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs in Hong Kong told CNN they had been unable to access email and Teams throughout the day.

Japan’s government returned to paper-based processes after ministries struggled to send emails for much of Friday. Australia’s spy agency and federal police were also among the affected organisations.

The Philippine Supreme Court warned of delays, while Australian schools and courts reported email disruptions. US city governments, including Miami Beach and Austin, asked residents to use phone services instead. A Colorado sheriff’s office said the outage had delayed bond payments for prisoners.

Airlines including IndiGo and Akasa lost email support channels, while electric vehicle maker Workhorse postponed its earnings call because of business disruptions. Financial institutions, including Standard Chartered and ING Australia, also warned customers about scammers impersonating technical support staff and attempting to exploit the disruption.

The disruption has extended to AI services that rely on Microsoft’s productivity infrastructure. Both OpenAI and Anthropic have reported problems with their Microsoft 365 connectors, which allow their AI assistants to access workplace information such as emails, calendars, Teams conversations and SharePoint files.

OpenAI said it was investigating elevated errors affecting its Microsoft 365 connector. The company warned that new connections could fail and that existing tools might not work as expected.

Anthropic reported similar problems with Claude’s Microsoft 365 connector. Mail, calendar and search requests were failing for most users, while some users were also unable to open Claude for Outlook or use its mail and calendar functions.

Anthropic traced the problem to an upstream provider and subsequently confirmed that it was caused by the Microsoft 365 service incident.

The disruption does not mean that ChatGPT or Claude are entirely offline. The problems concern their connections to Microsoft’s services, rather than their underlying AI models. Anthropic’s status page lists the Claude API and Claude Code as operational, although Claude.ai and Claude Cowork have also been reporting degraded performance.

The incidents illustrate how an outage affecting a major productivity platform can spread to third-party applications and AI assistants that depend on its infrastructure.

The likely cause of the disruption remains under investigation. Australia’s home affairs minister, Tony Burke, told reporters in Sydney that Microsoft believed it was dealing with something similar to the CrowdStrike incident in 2024, describing it as an update that had gone wrong, according to CNN.

Microsoft has not confirmed that explanation as the root cause, and its investigation has focused on affected servers and recent configuration changes, while its recovery efforts have centred on restoring capacity and stabilising the infrastructure.

The timing is particularly pointed for Europe, where the outage coincided with EU leaders meeting in Dublin to discuss reducing the continent’s dependence on foreign technology providers.

The 2024 CrowdStrike incident exposed the risks of relying on a small number of technology providers for critical services. The latest Microsoft disruption adds another example of how problems at a single infrastructure provider can affect organisations across industries and countries, including services built by other technology companies.

For businesses relying on Microsoft 365, the incident also raises questions about contingency planning. When email, calendars and workplace collaboration tools become unavailable, organisations can quickly lose access to the systems they depend on to communicate with customers, employees and partners.

As Microsoft’s recovery efforts continue, the outage is a reminder that cloud-based productivity services are interconnected, and that a failure in one part of the ecosystem can have consequences far beyond the company experiencing the technical problem.

#3188. Italy fines Meta €805m over Facebook’s access to Android photos

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg at a dinner with tech leaders in the State Dining Room of the White House in Washington, Sept. 4, 2025.

Italy’s data protection authority, the Garante, has fined Meta €805m, or about $887m. It says the Facebook app for Android accessed photos, videos and their metadata on Italian users’ phones without specific consent or proper notice.

The decision, first reported in English by Reuters, targets a gallery suggestions feature available since 2023. While users scroll Facebook, it offers photos and videos from their phone as ideas for posts.

The Garante found that Facebook asked for gallery access with one permission for the whole app. That request followed a vague prompt to enable other features. Users could not tell they were also switching on gallery suggestions.

The regulator said about 20 million Android users in Italy were affected. It also weighed a 2019 decision against Meta and what it called poor cooperation. Changes Meta made after the complaint counted in its favour, but the Garante called them late and limited to users who update the app.

The fine equals about 0.47% of Meta’s global turnover. Within 60 days, Meta must ask for separate, specific consent for the feature. It must also keep the feature off by default, even for users who already granted access.

The probe did not examine whether gallery content was used to train AI, which Meta denies. The Garante will look separately at a cloud processing feature launched in 2026.

The penalty is close to the €825m Dutch fine on Uber, though below Meta’s €1.2bn GDPR fine over data transfers. Meta is also tangling with Italy over a ruling on publisher payments.

Reuters said Meta was not immediately available for comment.

The Innocn E49M1R delivers massive, dual-27-inch screen real estate in a unique flat form factor, backed by punchy Mini-LED backlighting and plenty of ports. The lack of USB-C Power Delivery and edge wash-out from sitting too close hold it back slightly — though if you have a deep desk and run a desktop PC, there’s no monitor quite like it.

Widest, flat super ultrawide monitor available

Deep blacks thanks to Mini-LED backlighting

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

The Innocn E49M1R isn’t your standard super ultrawide monitor. Instead of a curved panel like on other popular massive displays, it’s completely flat and gives you the screen real estate of two 27-inch, 1440p monitors running across your desk.

When connected to your PC or Mac, you can have two full-sized browser windows or apps running side by side. This makes the E49M1R an excellent choice for productivity, though with a 165Hz panel, Mini-LED backlighting, and AMD FreeSync Premium, it also provides a very immersive gaming experience — granted you have a PC powerful enough to run games at this monitor’s native resolution.

I’ve been using the E49M1R as my daily driver for a month now, and it’s definitely changed how I work. While I’ve used a standard 21:9 ultrawide display for almost a decade, jumping to 32:9 and all that extra screen space has made a real difference while multitasking. Still, it has its trade-offs. While this monitor offers dual HDMI and DisplayPort connections, it’s missing a USB-C port for a one-cable connection to your laptop. Likewise, due to its VA panel and sheer width, colors can appear washed out at the edges if you’re sitting too close.

My Innocn E49M1R review will help you decide if this is the best monitor for your workflow and your desk, or if it’s worth going with something smaller or slightly curved instead.

2 x HDMI 2.1, 2 x DisplayPort 1.4, 1 x audio out, 2 x USB-A, 1 x USB-B

47.82 × 1.99 × 14.43 inches (without stand), 47.82 × 9.31 × 21.44 inches (with stand)

The Innocn E49M1R is truly one of a kind, as there’s no other flat super ultrawide display this large. It takes up the full width of most desks, but in return, you get an impressively bright picture, plenty of screen real estate, enough input ports to connect four devices at once, and built-in speakers for the complete package.

At 47.82 x 1.99 x 14.43 inches, the E49M1R is the largest monitor I’ve ever unboxed. Just like with a large TV, I’d recommend having someone help you unpack it and install the included metal stand. In addition, you also get a power cord, an HDMI 2.1 cable, and a DisplayPort cable in the box. Unfortunately, there isn’t a USB-B cable included, which you’ll need if you want to take advantage of the E49M1R’s built-in USB hub — more on that later.

Just like with the other Innocn monitors I’ve tested, installing the metal stand is a breeze. It simply snaps into the back of the monitor, and a single thumb screw attaches the arm to its sturdy metal base. If you’d rather use one of the best monitor arms instead of the included stand, there are 100 x 100 VESA mounting holes on the back of the display.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

One thing I really appreciate about the E49M1R is that instead of tucking all the ports on the underside like you often see on other monitors, they’re all positioned on the back. Along with being height-adjustable, the stand features a cutout near the bottom to make routing cables up to the display easier.

Port-wise, you get dual HDMI 2.1 inputs and dual DisplayPort 1.4 connections, alongside an audio jack. There’s also a USB-B upstream port that, when connected to your computer, lets you use the two USB-A ports next to it for wireless dongles or a webcam. This isn’t a KVM (keyboard, video, mouse) switch, though, as you can’t share those peripherals across two separate computers. At the same time, there’s no USB-C port with Power Delivery, which feels like an odd omission on a premium, super ultrawide monitor like the E49M1R.

With the E49M1R unboxed and the stand installed, it was time to get it set up on my desk. Now a word of warning here — if you have a desk that’s 48 inches wide, you likely won’t have room for a full desktop PC, though you could tuck one of the best mini PCs underneath this massive display.

I set the E49M1R up on a desk shelf attached to the back of the Secretlab Magnus Evo, and even though that desk is 60 inches wide, things still felt a bit cramped. Fortunately, I’m in the process of reviewing the GMKtec Evo-X3, which is quite thin and designed to be used vertically.

So what’s it like sitting in front of a massive, 49-inch flat super ultrawide? It was definitely daunting at first, but after a few hours, my eyes and neck adjusted to the larger display. By default, you can position one app or browser window on either side, and this felt a lot like the dual-monitor setup I put together last year — just without a gap between the two screens.

While using the E49M1R with two Chrome windows side by side worked well enough, it wasn’t until I installed Microsoft’s PowerToys utility that I could take full advantage of this monitor. Using PowerToys’ built-in FancyZones window manager, I was able to split this 49-inch display into thirds, keeping a smaller window for video calls in the middle with two larger browser windows on either side for multitasking. This worked great, as I could look straight at the center of the screen while presenting and glance off to the side when I needed to check notes or respond to a quick message.

As someone who’s been using an ultrawide monitor for years, making the jump from 21:9 to 32:9 felt natural. If you’ve been using a standard 16:9 display on its own, though, you might be better off switching to a 21:9 ultrawide first before going all the way up to a super ultrawide — especially with a completely flat one like the E49M1R.

One thing you’ll likely have to deal with when switching to an ultrawide — or even a super ultrawide — monitor is black bars on the sides of most video content. However, when you find a video with the right aspect ratio for your screen, it’s a sight to behold.

To put the E49M1R’s video capabilities to the test, I scoured YouTube for 32:9 trailers until I found one for Godzilla vs. Kong. Seeing King Kong leaping across the landscape and fighting in Hollow Earth was downright awesome, and even though this was a compressed YouTube stream, the picture still looked fantastic on the E49M1R.

Based on our lab tests, you can see that while the E49M1R isn’t as bright as some other premium monitors when displaying content in SDR, it absolutely shines with HDR enabled — hitting a blistering 1,474 nits. It did fairly well with color accuracy, though this is a productivity monitor, and I wouldn’t recommend it for color grading or other heavy graphical work.

While 32:9 videos may be hard to find online, the same can’t be said for games. With a powerful gaming PC, you can fully immerse yourself in the action across the E49M1R’s entire 49-inch display.

Even though it was a tight fit, I managed to get the GMKtec Neo-X1 Pro set up on the side of the E49M1R and play some Red Dead Redemption 2. Riding on my horse across the Wild West as Arthur Morgan felt almost like a dream come true, as I could take in all the scenery thanks to the E49M1R’s wider field of view. I’m sure playing a racing game like Forza Horizon 6 would have been even better, though.

It’s worth noting that while the E49M1R has a 165Hz refresh rate with support for AMD FreeSync Premium, the display definitely lags behind the best gaming monitors when it comes to response time. At 8ms, it’s better suited for slower-paced games, which is why I tested it out with Red Dead Redemption 2 as opposed to a fast-paced, competitive shooter.

All in all, though, you can certainly play games on the E49M1R — even if it’s ultimately better suited for multi-window productivity tasks.

There’s truly no super ultrawide monitor quite like the Innocn E49M1R, thanks to its massive, completely flat display. However, that sheer width can cause colors on either side to look washed out depending on how close you’re sitting, and a USB-C port would have been a welcome addition.

Although this is the first super ultrawide monitor I’ve tested, I’ve actually spent quite a bit of time using two of Innocn’s ultrawide displays: the 40C1U and the 40C1R. While the former is a premium display with a 5K2K resolution and the latter is a more budget-friendly gaming monitor, both feature USB-C with Power Delivery.

Unfortunately, the E49M1R doesn’t. Now, I know some budget laptops would struggle to drive a massive display like this one, but most modern machines can handle it just fine. With Power Delivery built in, you also wouldn’t need to reach for your laptop charger — instead, you could just plug in your Windows laptop or MacBook and get right to work on the E49M1R’s 49-inch screen.

For a monitor with a list price of $999, the lack of a USB-C port is really puzzling, especially since I’ve tested much cheaper displays from Innocn that have one.

Now, whether you prefer a flat or curved ultrawide is something you’ll have to figure out on your own. Personally, I like flat ultrawides since they take up less space on my desk and can easily be wall-mounted or attached to a monitor arm.

With the E49M1R and its VA panel, however, its massive width creates a sort of optical illusion. Even though the picture on either side is just as bright as it is at the center, it doesn’t always appear that way — particularly when you’re sitting very close to the display. For instance, with three Chrome windows side by side, content on the outer two would appear washed out when I turned my head to look at it. However, if I pulled my office chair back a bit, it looked completely normal.

Now, if you’re dead set on having the largest, flattest super ultrawide monitor out there, I’d recommend pairing the E49M1R with a very deep desk. That way, you can position the monitor at the very back edge to mitigate this optical illusion. If you’re short on space, though, and aren’t using one of the best standing desks, you could always wall-mount this display just like you would a TV.

The Innocn E49M1R is truly one of a kind, and it’s a great fit for those who want as much screen real estate as possible without a multi-monitor setup or having to give up desk space for a curved display. That alone would be enough, but its Mini-LED backlighting really makes colors pop and blacks appear deeper, too. You also get plenty of ports alongside a built-in USB hub.

While I would have liked a built-in KVM switch as well, that isn’t necessarily a dealbreaker. Missing a USB-C port with Power Delivery could be a problem if you’re mainly a laptop user — though if you primarily use a desktop computer, this won’t be an issue, even if it still would have been a nice addition.

The Innocn E49M1R delivers and then some for anyone who wants the widest, flattest super ultrawide monitor you can get. At full price, you’re getting plenty of screen space for your buck — just make sure this display isn’t too wide for your setup and that you have a desk big enough to house it first.

#3186. Apple reportedly met with Thai officials over spyware alerts sent to politicians

Bloomberg reports that Apple has met with Thai government officials in the wake of its recent wave of iPhone alerts about mercenary spyware attacks. Here are the details.

Last week, The Financial Times and TechCrunch reported that Apple had sent a fresh wave of threat notifications to potential spyware targets in 99 countries, warning them that they may have been targeted by mercenary spyware attacks.

At the time, the FT focused on German lawmakers who had received the warnings, while TechCrunch highlighted recipients in other countries, including Beirut-based filmmaker Radwan Mortada.

Today, Bloomberg reported that “Thailand held meetings with Apple Inc. officials” over the notifications, adding that the warnings raised questions about “who may have targeted [Thai politicians] and why.”

Receiving an alert doesn’t necessarily mean a device was successfully compromised, Digital Economy and Society Minister Chaichanok Chidchob said after meeting Apple representatives Wednesday, Krungthep Turakij and other media reported. Thai authorities also have no evidence so far that the latest attempted attacks involved Pegasus, the spyware developed by Israel’s NSO Group, he said.

As Bloomberg explains, Pegasus was “allegedly used against pro-democracy campaigners in 2022.”

The recent wave of alerts, which were sent out on October 29, followed another round in August, when Apple notified potential targets in 110 countries. As always, Apple declined to disclose what triggers these notifications to prevent attackers from evading detection in the future, but recommended that recipients enable Lockdown Mode and seek expert security assistance.

Bloomberg added that Thai authorities are expected to meet with other technology companies on Thursday to discuss potential countermeasures, including risks to Android devices.

#3185. Jensen Huang struggled to reach Beijing’s chip policymakers, FT says

Nvidia had no dedicated China government team until late 2025, and Beijing’s security camp won the argument over its chips.

NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang during his GTC 2026 keynote at the SAP Center in San Jose, 16 March 2026

Jensen Huang spent years courting China, but he struggled to reach the officials who decided Nvidia’s fate there, the Financial Times reported. The paper cited people familiar with the matter.

Huang resigned as Nvidia’s chief executive on Thursday. He had admitted an affair with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive whom US officials suspect of spying for China. Beijing denies she is a spy, and the two are not related.

The FT looks at what came before. Huang visited China six times in three years. His first recorded meeting with a top leader came in April 2025, with Vice-Premier He Lifeng. In July 2025 he met He again, and commerce minister Wang Wentao too.

Those meetings ran through Ren Hongbin, who heads China’s main trade promotion body, the FT said. But Nvidia never secured talks with the National Development and Reform Commission. The FT says the state planner led Beijing’s push to restrict Nvidia chips.

Huang also failed to win more time with Wang once those curbs arrived. Part of the problem was Nvidia’s thin lobbying, the FT said. It had no dedicated team for Chinese officials until late 2025, when it hired Tony Jiang from Intel.

Beijing was also split, according to the paper. The commerce ministry saw Nvidia chips as a bridge while Huawei caught up. Security officials saw reliance on Nvidia as a weakness, and their view has gained ground over the past year.

Huang often warned Washington that export curbs would only help Huawei. Now some say his exit will do the same.

“It may sound ironic, but the fall of Jensen helps to strengthen Huawei’s leading position in China,” George Chen, a partner at the Asia Group, told the FT.

In May, Huang joined President Donald Trump’s business delegation to China. He briefly spoke with Xi Jinping and Premier Li Qiang, the most senior leaders he had met in public.

Nvidia, the commerce ministry and China’s cyberspace regulator did not respond to the FT. Nvidia’s board inquiry continues, and it reports third-quarter results on 17 November.

#3183. Binance warns iPhone crypto holders of security flaw researchers say remains unpatched

Crypto exchange Binance has warned iPhone users about an iOS vulnerability that could allow malicious apps to access sensitive data stored by other apps. Here are the details.

In a post published on X (via AppleInsider), Binance says that a vulnerability called worse_query could allow “malicious apps to read local files from other apps, putting seed phrases, private keys, and login credentials at risk across the entire ecosystem.”

Binance says the flaw affects iOS 26.7.1, iOS 27.0.1, and iOS 27.2. However, a Community Note points out that researchers describe the vulnerability as an unpatched zero-day and that Apple’s latest security updates, including iOS 27.2.1 (the current version at the time of writing), do not mention a fix.

A vulnerability (worse_query) affecting iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1, and 27.2 allows malicious apps to read local files from other apps, putting seed phrases, private keys, and login credentials at risk across the entire ecosystem. This is an iOS-level issue, not unique to Binance.…

That said, in addition to updating their devices, Binance recommends that iPhone crypto holders take the following immediate actions:

The vulnerability was disclosed by security researchers @0xjohnny and @forcequitOS, who published a proof of concept on GitHub demonstrating how it can be used to bypass iOS sandbox protections, which normally prevent apps from accessing each other’s files.

Researcher @forcequitOS also noted that neither iOS 27.2.1 nor iOS 27.3 beta 1 patches the vulnerability.

Just as a general statement so there isn’t any confusion about it, worse_query is *not* patched in iOS 27.2.1 and 27.3 beta 1. I’ll update version support on the readme when it’s patched.

Although the researcher describes the code as intended for developers and not useful on its own, other developers have already built apps using it, including a file manager that can access, modify, and delete data belonging to other apps without requiring a jailbreak.

According to The Hacker News, neither Binance nor the researchers have reported any attacks or cryptocurrency thefts involving the vulnerability so far.

#3182. Sony: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Sony's TSMC tie-up is meant to protect its image sensor leadership, a bet that scale and cost control can hold up as mobile competition tightens.

On its second-quarter fiscal year 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 5, 2026, Sony (SONY +1.54%) announced that consolidated operating income rose 45% year over year to 622.3 billion Japanese yen. For long-term investors, the business is shifting toward recurring digital services and proprietary content licensing, which reduces reliance on hardware upgrade cycles. Three takeaways from the call stand out.

Hardware unit sales gradually decline as gaming consoles mature, but digital ecosystem engagement keeps expanding. Platform user activity reached record levels for September, showing that high-margin digital software and network subscription revenues can protect profitability as hardware sales slow.

Older music releases generate steady cash flow without requiring upfront production spending. Digital streaming services broaden the audience for historical music releases, creating enduring royalty streams that require minimal capital expenditure to maintain.

Mobile device markets face inventory shifts and component pricing pressures, raising costs across manufacturing. Joining forces with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) gives the image sensor division essential manufacturing scale and technology depth to defend market leadership.

Distribution platforms and high-profile intellectual property (IP) drive operating income past 1 trillion yen in the first half of fiscal year 2026 for the first time in Sony's history. Global distribution channels like the PlayStation Network and the Crunchyroll anime streaming service create synergies with blockbuster films and music tracks, shielding cash flow against high inflation.

Strategic capital allocation prioritizes long-term growth across entertainment and semiconductor assets while preserving corporate balance sheet health. The upcoming mid-range corporate plan aims to capture broader ecosystem synergies.

#3181. iPhone Duo one week later: The future, or not for me?

My iPhone Duo arrived last Thursday, so I’ve had a week to use it as my daily carry. My early experience has been mixed, so I keep asking myself an important question: is this the iPhone’s future and I just need to adapt, or is the Duo simply not for everyone?

After a week using the iPhone Duo, in some ways I have a lot of clarity about the product, and in other ways my thinking is very clouded.

To put it simply: I’m not having a great time with the Duo, which makes me wonder if the problem is me, not it.

I’ve seen countless social media posts from Duo owners proclaiming how much they love the product. And I absolutely believe them. The iPhone Duo is a remarkable innovation for the iPhone. It’s cool, weird, and wonderful in all sorts of ways. But for me and my needs (preferences?), it’s been more frustrating than enjoyable.

And that frustration mainly boils down to one thing: I almost never want to open it.

I’d estimate at least 90% of my iPhone Duo usage involves the front display. And when I unfold it the remaining 10% of the time, it’s often because I force myself to do it in the hopes of discovering what I’m missing out on. Like, I know I should be unfolding it more, so I do. But it doesn’t add any real value for me.

Because I rarely want to open the iPhone Duo, I’m left using the outer display all the time. In that mode, the Duo is too heavy for extended use, too wide to comfortably reach, and the UI in most apps is an adjustment.

Are these dealbreakers? No. I could live with the Duo’s outer display if I had to, but it’s definitely an inferior experience to my iPhone 18 Pro.

If I was opening the iPhone Duo more, and actually taking advantage of the key value proposition of foldables—that you can unfold them—I doubt the outer screen would bother me much.

But what I’ve found, at least so far, is that one-handed iPhone use is very important to me, which rules out using the inner display. I use my iPhone mostly for quick interactions, and often with a child in one hand (I have three very young kids). In situations when I do have two hands free to open the Duo, I’m probably sitting in front of my iPad Pro with a Magic Keyboard attached and would rather use the iPad instead.

So again: is the problem with the Duo, or with me?

I think foldables and slab phones will obviously coexist as there will be fans of each.

I’m absolutely already converted however and am loving my duo.

Considering the Air was my favourite phone up until this it’s surprised me. I love proper one handed use again on the outside screen and unfolded it’s much nicer than my old mini 7.

I get it’s not for everyone but those that click with it like myself have a superb device!

I think it’s the latter, but I’m not sure “problem” is the right word. I just don’t find myself using it the way it’s meant to be used. And that’s fine.

I want to love the iPhone Duo, because I see how much fun other people are having with it. And maybe given more time, something will click and I’ll start to use it “as intended.”

If iPhone Duo is the future of the iPhone, I’ll adapt and move on with my life. But one week in, I think it’s probably just not for me. And if it’s not for me, maybe there are a lot of people who will continue preferring non-foldable iPhones for many years to come.

What’s your iPhone Duo experience been like? Are you loving it or struggling? Let us know in the comments.

#3180. OpenWorld (OPNW) Q4 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Real-world asset tokenization now drives most revenue as the platform scales.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

OpenWorld, Inc. (OPNW -5.24%) reported its first quarterly results following a reverse takeover, highlighting a strategic transition toward high-margin real-world asset (RWA) tokenization. Management reported that the company is shifting away from project-based activity to focus on long-term platform-oriented infrastructure and recurring revenue. The financial results were impacted by significant nonrecurring costs related to the public listing and noncash stock-based compensation, though underlying operations generated positive adjusted EBITDA. The company also confirmed it is advancing a pipeline of large-scale tokenized financing programs totaling more than $1.1 billion across the artificial intelligence, energy, and intellectual property sectors.

Please refer to our earnings release for an explanation of these measures and how we use them, and in the case of the non-GAAP financial measures, reconciliations to their nearest GAAP equivalents. With that, it's now my pleasure to turn the call over to Matt Shaw. Matt, please go ahead.

Matt Shaw: Thank you, Richard, and good afternoon, everyone. Thank you for joining us. I'm Matt Shaw, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of OpenWorld. This is our first earnings call as a combined company following the reverse acquisition that closed on September 30. I'd like to welcome all of our investors, those who have been with us through the VerifyMe chapter, those who have joined us from the OpenWorld side, and our new shareholders who have come on board since the merger. We're happy to have all of you with us for what we expect will be a very bright future for the company and our shareholders.

Before we get into the Q3 results and recent developments, let me set the stage for how we approached building our platform. Since early this year, we have seen a clear and accelerating uptake in interest in real-world asset tokenization from some of the largest companies in the world. What began as initial exploratory conversations around how we can bring value to our partners is now starting to formalize into term sheets and definitive agreements. That is exactly the progression we designed the business to capture. Our anchor deals, those we intend to scale from, are taking shape across the U.S., the Middle East, and we expect soon in Southeast Asia.

These are the geographies where we see the strongest near-term opportunity to move from signed term sheets into capital formation and platform deployment. With that context, I will now turn the call over to our Chief Financial Officer, Gerard Hernandez, who will walk you through the financial results for the third quarter. After Gerard, our President, Russ McMeekin, will take you through the build-out of our RWA pipeline from signed term sheets through the start of capital formation and give you a preview of what is coming next. Gerard, over to you.

Gerard Hernandez: Thank you, Matt. Good afternoon, everyone, and thank you for joining us. I will review our third quarter results with particular focus on the substantial growth in our real-world asset business and the nature of certain non-recurring expenses we incurred in the period. The quarter's results clearly reflect OpenWorld's strategic priorities. We have been deliberately shifting the business from project-based token launch activity toward higher value, recurring, long-term arrangement, and platform-oriented real-world asset infrastructure and tokenization services. That strategic focus is visible in the third quarter numbers, which we believe are just the starting point for what our business model can deliver consistently going forward. For the three months ended September 30, 2026, total revenue was $7.4 million.

Of that amount, real-world asset platform revenues contributed $6.4 million, or approximately 86% of quarterly revenue. There was no RWA revenue in Q3 2025, as our ramp-up of RWA revenue only began in early 2026. We see significant opportunities to continue growing our RWA business over the coming quarters and years. The Q3 revenue performance represents major growth and is a direct reflection of the strategy we have been executing against. For the first nine months of 2026, RWA revenue reached $9.1 million. As of September 30, approximately $21.2 million of transaction price remained allocated to unsatisfied or partially unsatisfied performance obligations under our RWA arrangements, providing visibility into future revenue recognition as these contractual performance obligations are satisfied.

Digital assets and capital markets revenue was $0.4 million in the quarter, down from the $20 million in Q3 2025. Much of which was one-time revenue associated with specific token generation events last year. Gross profit in the quarter was $6.3 million, producing a gross margin of 84%, up from 77% a year ago, driven by those higher margin mix from the RWA work. Turning to expenses, our third quarter results were significantly impacted by costs associated with a reverse takeover transaction and one-time non-cash stock-based compensation. General and administrative expenses totaled $14.6 million.

Within that amount, $6 million consisted of professional fees associated with RTO and public listing process, and $6.4 million was stock-based compensation from option and restricted share grants. These two items accounted for the majority of quarterly G&A expenses, reflecting significant transaction-weighted costs and non-cash stock-based compensation. Other operating expenses were modest. Management technology of $0.9 million, research and development of $0.4 million, and sales and marketing of $0.5 million. As a result, we recorded a net loss of $10.2 million or $0.93 per share. #3177. Atomically Thin Materials Significantly Shrink Qubits

MIT researchers use 2D materials for capacitors in quantum circuits in an effort to scale processors

Superconducting quantum processor and its microwave packaging.

Quantum computing is a devilishly complex technology, with many technical hurdles impacting its development. Of these challenges two critical issues stand out: miniaturization and qubit quality.

IBM has adopted the superconducting qubit road map of reaching a 1,121-qubit processor by 2023, leading to the expectation that 1,000 qubits with today’s qubit form factor is feasible. However, current approaches will require very large chips (50 millimeters on a side, or larger) at the scale of small wafers, or the use of chiplets on multichip modules. While this approach will work, the aim is to attain a better path toward scalability.

Now researchers at MIT have been able to both reduce the size of the qubits and done so in a way that reduces the interference that occurs between neighboring qubits. The MIT researchers have increased the number of superconducting qubits that can be added onto a device by a factor of 100.

“We are addressing both qubit miniaturization and quality,” said William Oliver, the director for the Center for Quantum Engineering at MIT. “Unlike conventional transistor scaling, where only the number really matters, for qubits, large numbers are not sufficient, they must also be high-performance. Sacrificing performance for qubit number is not a useful trade in quantum computing. They must go hand in hand.”

The key to this big increase in qubit density and reduction of interference comes down to the use of two-dimensional materials, in particular the 2D insulator hexagonal boron nitride (hBN). The MIT researchers demonstrated that a few atomic monolayers of hBN can be stacked to form the insulator in the capacitors of a superconducting qubit.

Just like other capacitors, the capacitors in these superconducting circuits take the form of a sandwich in which an insulator material is sandwiched between two metal plates. The big difference for these capacitors is that the superconducting circuits can operate only at extremely low temperatures—less than 0.02 degrees above absolute zero (-273.15 °C).

Superconducting qubits are measured at temperatures as low as 20 millikelvin in a dilution refrigerator.Nathan Fiske/MIT

In that environment, insulating materials that are available for the job, such as PE-CVD silicon oxide or silicon nitride, have quite a few defects that are too lossy for quantum computing applications. To get around these material shortcomings, most superconducting circuits use what are called coplanar capacitors. In these capacitors, the plates are positioned laterally to one another, rather than on top of one another.

As a result, the intrinsic silicon substrate below the plates and to a smaller degree the vacuum above the plates serve as the capacitor dielectric. Intrinsic silicon is chemically pure and therefore has few defects, and the large size dilutes the electric field at the plate interfaces, all of which leads to a low-loss capacitor. The lateral size of each plate in this open-face design ends up being quite large (typically 100 by 100 micrometers) in order to achieve the required capacitance.

In an effort to move away from the large lateral configuration, the MIT researchers embarked on a search for an insulator that has very few defects and is compatible with superconducting capacitor plates.

“We chose to study hBN because it is the most widely used insulator in 2D material research due to its cleanliness and chemical inertness,” said colead author Joel Wang, a research scientist in the Engineering Quantum Systems group of the MIT Research Laboratory for Electronics.

On either side of the hBN, the MIT researchers used the 2D superconducting material, niobium diselenide. One of the trickiest aspects of fabricating the capacitors was working with the niobium diselenide, which oxidizes in seconds when exposed to air, according to Wang. This necessitates that the assembly of the capacitor occur in a glove box filled with argon gas.

While this would seemingly complicate the scaling up of the production of these capacitors, Wang doesn’t regard this as a limiting factor.

“What determines the quality factor of the capacitor are the two interfaces between the two materials,” said Wang. “Once the sandwich is made, the two interfaces are “sealed” and we don’t see any noticeable degradation over time when exposed to the atmosphere.”

This lack of degradation is because around 90 percent of the electric field is contained within the sandwich structure, so the oxidation of the outer surface of the niobium diselenide does not play a significant role anymore. This ultimately makes the capacitor footprint much smaller, and it accounts for the reduction in cross talk between the neighboring qubits.

“The main challenge for scaling up the fabrication will be the wafer-scale growth of hBN and 2D superconductors like [niobium diselenide], and how one can do wafer-scale stacking of these films,” added Wang.

Wang believes that this research has shown 2D hBN to be a good insulator candidate for superconducting qubits. He says that the groundwork the MIT team has done will serve as a road map for using other hybrid 2D materials to build superconducting circuits.

Dexter Johnson is a contributing editor at IEEE Spectrum, with a focus on nanotechnology.

#3176. Gentler Streak 6.0 adds a new wellbeing timeline and customizable dashboard

In an update rolling out today, Gentler Streak is introducing new ways for users to track their wellbeing and personalize the app’s guidance based on how they feel. Here are the details.

One of my favorite exercise-tracking apps got even better today with an update that expands its functionality beyond workouts and fitness metrics to better reflect how users actually feel.

Starting today, Gentler Streak will let users log how they feel each day, including their mood, symptoms, and other factors that may not be reflected in their health and fitness data.

Some days, the way we feel isn’t reflected in what the data says, no matter the data quality. “How I Feel” captures the part that devices can’t grasp: personal context. And how you feel is not only a mood: it is also a sore throat, heavy legs or a poor night’s sleep. The feature was inspired by the Gentler Streak community, including people living with chronic fatigue, fibromyalgia, ADHD, and those not wearing their Apple Watch at night. Without overnight signals, their guidance has less to work with.

According to the team behind Gentler Streak, these new features are aimed at users whose health and fitness data may not accurately reflect how they feel, including those dealing with chronic conditions, menopause, stress, or poor sleep.

In practice, the app will now feature four tabs: Today, Health, Workouts, and Insights. In the Today and Health tabs, a new “Anything to add?” field will let users rate how they feel, from Great to Off, and add context about what might be affecting their well-being, including fatigue, feeling calm, or custom tags.

You decide when the prompt appears. Go to Profile > Settings > Self-Evaluation Prompt and choose one of three options: only when your vitals or sleep are off, always on, or never.

Gentler Stories notes that the self-assessments will override the app’s wellbeing estimates for that day, with its daily guidance adjusting accordingly.

The Today tab will also feature an expanded 10- or 30-day timeline showing logged workouts, wellbeing estimates, potential symptoms, poor sleep or vitals, and the first day of a menstrual period, while Health will introduce an interactive chart showing users how their wellbeing changes over time, with the ability to filter by symptoms.

Users can now also customize which information appears on their Today screen, including vitals, sleep, steps, menstrual cycle, VO₂ max, and workouts, which is a nice touch.

For users who are sick, injured, or taking a break from exercise, the app’s hallmark Activity Path will make way for a new Wellbeing Path, which lets them track their wellbeing on a daily basis.

For users with Active status, a new colorful wellbeing line will appear beneath the Activity Path, reflecting how they feel each day. This information is logged automatically for those who wear their Apple Watch overnight, or based on self-assessments for those who don’t.

Importantly, Gentler Stories notes that all information entered through the new feature remains on the user’s device, with no accounts or company-operated servers involved.

Gentler Streak is available for free on the App Store, with in-app purchases for monthly, yearly, family, and lifetime subscriptions.

#3174. How AI Will Change Chip Design

Artificial intelligence’s promise and potential for the semiconductor industry

Rina Diane Caballar is a contributing editor covering tech and its intersections with science, society, and the environment.

An array of semiconductor wafers are ready to be made into chips.

The end of Moore’s Law is looming. Engineers and designers can do only so much to miniaturize transistors and pack as many of them as possible into chips. So they’re turning to other approaches to chip design, incorporating technologies like AI into the process.

Samsung, for instance, is adding AI to its memory chips to enable processing in memory, thereby saving energy and speeding up machine learning. Speaking of speed, Google’s TPU V4 AI chip has doubled its processing power compared with that of its previous version.

But AI holds still more promise and potential for the semiconductor industry. To better understand how AI is set to revolutionize chip design, we spoke with Heather Gorr, senior product manager for MathWorks’ MATLAB platform.

How is AI currently being used to design the next generation of chips?

Heather Gorr: AI is such an important technology because it’s involved in most parts of the cycle, including the design and manufacturing process. There’s a lot of important applications here, even in the general process engineering where we want to optimize things. I think defect detection is a big one at all phases of the process, especially in manufacturing. But even thinking ahead in the design process, [AI now plays a significant role] when you’re designing the light and the sensors and all the different components. There’s a lot of anomaly detection and fault mitigation that you really want to consider.

Then, thinking about the logistical modeling that you see in any industry, there is always planned downtime that you want to mitigate; but you also end up having unplanned downtime. So, looking back at that historical data of when you’ve had those moments where maybe it took a bit longer than expected to manufacture something, you can take a look at all of that data and use AI to try to identify the proximate cause or to see something that might jump out even in the processing and design phases. We think of AI oftentimes as a predictive tool, or as a robot doing something, but a lot of times you get a lot of insight from the data through AI.

What are the benefits of using AI for chip design?

Gorr: Historically, we’ve seen a lot of physics-based modeling, which is a very intensive process. We want to do a reduced order model, where instead of solving such a computationally expensive and extensive model, we can do something a little cheaper. You could create a surrogate model, so to speak, of that physics-based model, use the data, and then do your parameter sweeps, your optimizations, your Monte Carlo simulations using the surrogate model. That takes a lot less time computationally than solving the physics-based equations directly. So, we’re seeing that benefit in many ways, including the efficiency and economy that are the results of iterating quickly on the experiments and the simulations that will really help in the design.

So it’s like having a digital twin in a sense?

Gorr: Exactly. That’s pretty much what people are doing, where you have the physical system model and the experimental data. Then, in conjunction, you have this other model that you could tweak and tune and try different parameters and experiments that let sweep through all of those different situations and come up with a better design in the end.

So, it’s going to be more efficient and, as you said, cheaper?

Gorr: Yeah, definitely. Especially in the experimentation and design phases, where you’re trying different things. That’s obviously going to yield dramatic cost savings if you’re actually manufacturing and producing [the chips]. You want to simulate, test, experiment as much as possible without making something using the actual process engineering.

We’ve talked about the benefits. How about the drawbacks?

Gorr: The [AI-based experimental models] tend to not be as accurate as physics-based models. Of course, that’s why you do many simulations and parameter sweeps. But that’s also the benefit of having that digital twin, where you can keep that in mind—it’s not going to be as accurate as that precise model that we’ve developed over the years.

Both chip design and manufacturing are system intensive; you have to consider every little part. And that can be really challenging. It’s a case where you might have models to predict something and different parts of it, but you still need to bring it all together.

One of the other things to think about too is that you need the data to build the models. You have to incorporate data from all sorts of different sensors and different sorts of teams, and so that heightens the challenge.

How can engineers use AI to better prepare and extract insights from hardware or sensor data?

Gorr: We always think about using AI to predict something or do some robot task, but you can use AI to come up with patterns and pick out things you might not have noticed before on your own. People will use AI when they have high-frequency data coming from many different sensors, and a lot of times it’s useful to explore the frequency domain and things like data synchronization or resampling. Those can be really challenging if you’re not sure where to start.

One of the things I would say is, use the tools that are available. There’s a vast community of people working on these things, and you can find lots of examples [of applications and techniques] on GitHub or MATLAB Central, where people have shared nice examples, even little apps they’ve created. I think many of us are buried in data and just not sure what to do with it, so definitely take advantage of what’s already out there in the community. You can explore and see what makes sense to you, and bring in that balance of domain knowledge and the insight you get from the tools and AI.

What should engineers and designers consider when using AI for chip design?

Gorr: Think through what problems you’re trying to solve or what insights you might hope to find, and try to be clear about that. Consider all of the different components, and document and test each of those different parts. Consider all of the people involved, and explain and hand off in a way that is sensible for the whole team.

How do you think AI will affect chip designers’ jobs?

Gorr: It’s going to free up a lot of human capital for more advanced tasks. We can use AI to reduce waste, to optimize the materials, to optimize the design, but then you still have that human involved whenever it comes to decision-making. I think it’s a great example of people and technology working hand in hand. It’s also an industry where all people involved—even on the manufacturing floor—need to have some level of understanding of what’s happening, so this is a great industry for advancing AI because of how we test things and how we think about them before we put them on the chip.

How do you envision the future of AI and chip design?

Gorr: It’s very much dependent on that human element—involving people in the process and having that interpretable model. We can do many things with the mathematical minutiae of modeling, but it comes down to how people are using it, how everybody in the process is understanding and applying it. Communication and involvement of people of all skill levels in the process are going to be really important. We’re going to see less of those superprecise predictions and more transparency of information, sharing, and that digital twin—not only using AI but also using our human knowledge and all of the work that many people have done over the years.

Rina Diane Caballar is a writer covering tech and its intersections with science, society, and the environment. An IEEE Spectrum contributing editor, she's a former software engineer based in New Zealand.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Katapult Holdings, Inc. (KPLT +8.21%) reported its first quarterly results following the merger of Katapult, Aaron's, and CCFI, a transaction that closed on Aug. 11, 2026. Management reported that the integration process has identified $30 million in annualized cost synergies, primarily through consolidated leadership, vendor rationalization, and shared corporate platforms. The company stated that it operates two primary segments: Consumer Finance and Lease-to-Own & Retail, serving a combined customer base of more than 2.1 million active users. Financial results for the quarter were influenced by merger-related costs and a higher interest expense environment. The company indicated that its strategic focus is centered on optimizing its proprietary data set for underwriting and simplifying its complex capital structure to reduce funding costs.
