#3148. Accelevation (ACCV) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Modular data center orders surged while margins and cash flow strengthened.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Accelevation Holdings Corp. (ACCV +5.82%) reported substantial growth in revenue and backlog during its first quarter as a public company, supported by a transition toward modular infrastructure solutions for data centers. Management stated that the operational strategy focused on domestic manufacturing and vertical integration, allowing for highly customized designs with industry-leading lead times. The company reported a significant broadening of its customer base and geographic footprint, reducing concentration risks while increasing the total content delivered per megawatt. Management confirmed the 2026 financial outlook and established mid-20% targets for recurring adjusted EBITDA margins over the medium term.

Operator: Good day, and thank you for standing by. Welcome to the Accelevation Q3 2026 Earnings Call. [Operator Instructions] Please be advised that today's conference is being recorded. I would now like to hand the conference over to your first speaker today, Larry De Maria. Please go ahead.

Lawrence De Maria: Thank you, operator. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us for Accelevation's Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Call, our first as a public company. I'm Larry De Maria, Senior Vice President of Investor Relations and Capital Markets. With me today are Michael Rubiera, our Founder and Chief Executive Officer; and Ken Krause, our Chief Financial Officer. The call is being webcast live on the Investor Relations section of our website at www.accelevation.com, where you will also find our earnings release and the presentation that accompanies today's remarks. A replay will be available on the same site following the call.

Let me remind you that today's presentation and remarks include forward-looking statements within the meaning of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995, including statements about our outlook, backlog, bookings, margins, cash flow and capital expenditures, capital structure and leverage, customer demand and diversification, capacity, new products and markets and growth plans. These statements are based on current expectations and assumptions and are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially from those expressed or implied. These risks, including those identified on Slide 2 of today's presentation in the Risk Factors section of our final prospectus for our initial public offering and in our other filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

Except as required by law, we undertake no obligation to update any forward-looking statement. We will also discuss certain non-GAAP financial measures, including adjusted EBITDA, adjusted EBITDA margin, adjusted net income, free cash flow and net leverage. These measures should be considered in addition to and not as a substitute for our GAAP results. Reconciliations to the most directly comparable GAAP measures are included in our earnings release and in the appendix to today's presentation. Michael will begin with an overview of Accelevation and the third quarter business update. Ken will then review our financial results, capital structure and the 2026 outlook. Michael will close with the key takeaways before we open the line for questions.

With that, I'll turn the call over to Michael.

Michael Rubiera: Thank you, Larry, and good morning, everyone. Today is a milestone for us, our first earnings call as a public company. To our new shareholders, welcome, and thank you for your confidence in Accelevation. And to our employees, thank you. You built the company investors see today, and you delivered the results we're going to walk through this morning. For those of you who are new to our story, my wife and I founded Accelevation in 2018 (sic) [ 2017 ] with a simple idea: build a U.S.-based manufacturing company that innovates and operates at the speed of technology. Today, we design, manufacture and install highly customized thermal infrastructure and electrical distribution products.

Our primary end market today is the domestic mission-critical data center build-out, and we sit at the critical point in that build-out. We custom design, manufacture and self-perform the installation of the complex integrated systems that are the last mile of construction, the final step before compute goes live and our customers can start generating revenue. Let's start with where we play. Our focus is the mission-critical white space, the server hall where power distribution, thermal management, airflow containment and structural systems power, cool and support the compute.

While this infrastructure is a relatively modest share of the total cost, it is the critical path to ensure our customers get to compute faster, start generating revenue sooner and avoid costly delays. Gray space is a natural adjacency and a real opportunity for us to expand our offerings beyond the white space over time. And while most of our business today is tied to data centers, most of the products are end-market agnostic, and we expect to target new markets as we grow. So what makes Accelevation different? We own the whole process from design through fabrication, installation and commissioning with one integrated team accountable from start to finish. We are not a standard product catalog company.

We co-design our solutions with our customers to meet their unique needs. That matters more every quarter. Projects have been getting bigger, deployment schedules keep compressing. And for our customers, a delay is not just a construction problem. It pushes back the moment their major investments in land, power and compute start generating revenue. Fragmented multi-vendor models add handoffs and add risk. Our model takes them out. Customers are buying speed to compute and certainty of execution, and you can see that in the 3 results on this slide. First, we have broadened our customer base. We added 7 significant new accounts in the third quarter alone across mission-critical end markets. This has also significantly diversified our customer base.

And at this point, only 2 customers represent a double-digit percentage of our bookings for the quarter, with our largest customer representing less than 20% of revenue for the third quarter. Within our core United States market, we are also working to diversify the states where we do business. Since we are in the last mile, we go where the customers need us and where power and permitting are not a risk. Second, we are winning a bigger share of each customer's wallet. We began shipments of our SkyBridge modular solution in late August, a product that comprises a significant amount of our backlog that did not exist in the first quarter.

By selling a complete modular unit that includes all of our products and services, we have seen our average order size grow 4x year-to-date versus a year ago. Third, we're investing in delivery and capacity ahead of expected need so that we are positioned to meet rapidly growing demand. The market is quickly shifting towards modular factory-built infrastructure. We positioned Accelevation for that shift. Our U.S. operating footprint has grown to approximately 1.5 million square feet, up from less than 170,000 square feet at the start of 2025. And we have built all of this efficiently with capital expenditures of approximately 3% of revenue year-to-date. Our domestic model makes that capacity even more valuable.

Our manufacturing and supply chain are predominantly U.S.-based and close to where our customers are building to enable us to respond faster and remain more agile than many of our competitors. For selective scopes, we can go from raw materials to shipment in as little as 24 hours. And we are investing in our people to match. Accelevation Academy builds skilled trades in-house, and our Built Together Ownership Program makes our employees owners of the company. I'll come back to that in the end. Put it all together, a broader customer base, a growing share of wallet and capacity in place ahead of expected demand, and you have a platform built for sustained profitable growth.

Now to the quarter, the headline. Our differentiated model delivered robust growth, solid profitability and strong cash flow generation, all in the same quarter. Revenue grew approximately 66% from prior year quarter to $202 million. Gross margins were 29.3%, while adjusted EBITDA was approximately $38 million, an 18.7% margin. Ken will take you through the details in a moment. And demand remains strong. Bookings in the quarter were approximately $770 million, up more than 350% year-over-year, bringing year-to-date bookings to approximately $1.9 billion and backlog to $1.7 billion. Book-to-bill was approximately 3.8x, our second consecutive quarter above 3x. Once again, orders materially outpaced revenue.

That expanded our backlog and increases our confidence in our 2026 guidance as well as our visibility into 2027. We also landed a major new relationship. This quarter, we received the largest order in our company's history from a new customer, with delivery expected over the next 6 to 12 months. That customer provided a significant upfront deposit, which strengthened our cash flow and liquidity. This customer first engaged us over the summer. They needed a new partner who could custom design a unique solution to their specific need, which will reduce their time to compute. Execution of the program is progressing as planned. We are also building to meet growing demand across all customer segments.

During the quarter, we opened Second Flight and broke ground on Third Flight, our next facility in Dayton, right next to our First and Second Flight facilities. Third Flight will add approximately 286,000 square feet and is expected to be operational by late summer 2027. It will add capacity ahead of demand, supported by our backlog and pipeline. It will expand our modular capabilities and gives us room to grow over -- our power products. Demand in the quarter was broad-based across our entire portfolio and customer segments. Our power products, which include remote power panels, branch circuit whips and power distribution units are strategically important.

They increase our content per installed megawatt and let us deliver a more complete scope as part of our modular solution and simplifies the total project complexity for our customers. Customers continue to prioritize modularity and prefabrication because moving work from the job site into controlled manufacturing environment reduces field labor, limits handoffs and improves schedule certainty. That momentum drove backlog to a record $1.7 billion, with a third quarter book-to-bill of 3.8x. In addition, our pipeline of new business remains healthy and gives us further confidence for 2027 and beyond.

As a reminder, our pipeline only includes projects where our engineering and solution teams are actively designing the specific white space solution for a specific job site that is already under construction with a hard time line requirements for delivery. That means those projects are beyond the permitting and electrification stage. And in many cases, we were the specified basis of design for the end customer. Now I know the financial markets have been volatile and investors continue to debate the pace and returns of AI infrastructure investment. So let me tell you what we're seeing from our customers. The demand signals remain strong. Strong orders, a record backlog, a healthy pipeline and continued demand for faster deployment.

Program timing, designs and site schedules can and will change, but our relatively short lead times, in-house engineering and domestic manufacturing position us to adapt while staying focused on the broader demand trend. We stay focused on what we can control. Internally, we call it winning in the turns, staying close to customers, executing with discipline and investing where we see the greatest long-term opportunities. Innovation is core to our DNA. In fact, over 80% of our third quarter product orders came from offerings we developed in the prior 12 months. That number says a lot about our culture. It is built on speed, agility and an entrepreneurial spirit.

We work behind the curtain with our customers to design solutions that solve their specific needs and challenges. And that means we become the specified basis of design for all of their projects and campuses. While we talk a lot about our patent-pending SkyBridge modular solution, the truth is it is just 1 of 8 unique platform designs today. This is what has allowed us to grow so rapidly and is the foundation of our future success. And our growth strategy goes well beyond any single product.

We see 5 reinforcing levers: 1, expand wallet share with our key blue-chip customers; 2, broaden the customer set and geographies; 3, increase power and thermal content per megawatt; 4, expand life cycle retrofit and maintenance services; and 5, selectively apply our capabilities in adjacent mission-critical electrical markets. Over time, we also intend to expand from our current white space focus into selected gray space solutions, where our design, manufacturing and installation model can create a similar advantage. We intend to pursue all of this with discipline. Finally, I want to come back to our people. Through the Built Together Ownership Program, more than 1,800 employees are now owners of this company. That alignment matters.

It drives retention, quality and the sense of urgency our customers feel every day. We move with the speed of technology and our employees think and act like owners. One more point on this because I know it matters to our shareholders. The majority of the cost of the Built Together is borne by our pre-IPO shareholders, who put the program in place. The remainder is funded through our standard equity incentive plan within the share reserve we laid out at the time of the IPO. So this program does not add dilution beyond what investors already saw in our prospectus.

Public shareholders get the benefit of a workforce of owners with the vast majority of the costs carried by the shareholders who came before them. I'm also pleased to announce the promotion of Ericka Harrison to Chief Commercial Officer. Ericka has been a key member of our leadership team and has led the critical manufacturing capacity expansion over the past few years. Before I hand it over, let me sum up. Record backlog, strong growth with solid profitability and cash generation, a broadening customer base and capacity in place ahead of demand. This is a strong start to our life as a public company, and we are excited about what is ahead. With that, I'll turn it over to Ken.

Kenneth Krause: Thank you, Michael, and good morning, everyone. We are pleased to deliver strong third quarter results, our first quarter as a public company. We delivered robust revenue growth, healthy margin levels, and we're positioned extremely well as we start the fourth quarter. Our customer base is starting to broaden. We are beginning to see projects in new geographies, and our pipeline of new business is very healthy. During my prepared comments, I will compare revenue with the prior year quarter and also discuss sequential performance, that's Q3 performance relative to Q2 of this year, which I believe provides the clearest view of our current operating trajectory as we scale.

Unless otherwise noted, balance sheet figures are as of September 30 and therefore, precede the closing of our IPO and refinancing that occurred in early October. We delivered a strong third quarter with revenue of approximately $202 million, up 66% year-over-year and more than 11% sequentially. During the quarter, we began ramping up production of our modular systems, moving away from our more traditional on-site assembly. We're just starting to see the benefits of this transition and expect continued growth and improved profitability in future quarters. With that said, growth continued to be broad-based and almost entirely organic, driven by backlog conversion, increased activity on newer programs and new customer contributions.

We're beginning to add new customers and penetrate new geographies, which are helping us build a more sustainable business model. No single customer accounted for more than 20% of revenue in the quarter, which is down considerably from prior quarters. Furthermore, states like Texas no longer comprise more than 50% of our business as we see demand in new states, like North Dakota, Wisconsin, Indiana and many others. Profitability improved from the second quarter with gross profit rising to $59 million from $48 million and gross margin expanding approximately 260 basis points to 29.3% from 26.7%.

Higher volume, pricing and a more favorable project mix drove the improvement, partially offset by certain inefficiencies associated with the initial modular production ramp and certain legacy projects. SG&A in the quarter was approximately $27 million or 13.1% of revenue. SG&A increased 68% year-over-year. And excluding approximately $5 million in recurring transaction costs and certain noncash items, SG&A would have increased much more modestly, reflecting controlled growth alongside our expanding revenue and customer base. Adjusted SG&A was about 11% of sales, in line with our low double-digit target. Sequential results highlight the platform's earnings potential.

Approximately $21 million in additional revenue generated about $11 million in additional gross profit and $13 million in additional adjusted EBITDA, representing incremental margins of roughly 52% and 63%, respectively. While we don't expect those incremental margins to repeat every quarter, they do, however, demonstrate the operating leverage available as we increase manufacturing utilization, spread fixed costs over higher volumes and shift towards more modular production. Adjusted EBITDA was approximately $38 million or 18.7% of revenue compared with approximately $25 million in the second quarter. Net income was about $3 million compared with a net loss of about $2.5 million in the second quarter. Adjusted net income was $21 million versus $15 million in Q2 2026.

Our earnings release and presentation provide the reconciliations and the items excluded from our non-GAAP measures. Cash generation was strong. Net cash provided by operating activities was approximately $63 million, and free cash flow was $55 million. Working capital benefited from the significant upfront customer deposit that Michael had mentioned previously. Customer deposits and milestone billing help align cash receipts with procurement and production requirements on larger programs, reducing the amount of capital required to support our growth. CapEx was 3.7% of revenue. We continue to target and expect CapEx at or below 3% of revenue going forward.

Our ability to expand in a capital-efficient manner, while customers help fund project working capital through deposits and milestone billing supports attractive returns on invested capital. As of September 30, cash and cash equivalents was approximately $109 million. Total debt was approximately $665 million, and net debt was approximately $557 million, using the definitions in our public presentation. The quarter end balance sheet reflects our prior credit facilities as the IPO and refinancing closed after quarter end. We incurred noncash debt extinguishment costs in October of $10 million to $11 million associated with the replacement of the pre-IPO credit facilities.

Following quarter end, we used the net primary proceeds of $171 million from the IPO and borrowings under new senior credit facilities to repay the prior credit agreement. The new facilities consist of a $400 million revolving credit facility and a $250 million Term Loan A, both of which are maturing in 2031. Pricing is SOFR plus 150 to 250 basis points following the initial pricing period compared with SOFR plus 450 to 525 basis points under the prior facilities. The refinancing materially reduces our cost of capital and improves our financial flexibility. We expect cash interest cost to approximately $8 million in the fourth quarter. At September 30, net leverage under the definition showed in our presentation was 4x.

Pro forma for the IPO and refinancing completed after quarter end, net leverage was below 3x. Our priorities are clear: support high-return organic growth while continuing to delever and build the financial profile of an investment-grade company over time. Transitioning to Slide 17. Today, we're introducing fiscal 2026 guidance. We expect revenue of $905 million to $915 million, up more than 100% at the midpoint versus 2025 and adjusted EBITDA of $155 million to $165 million, representing over 75% year-over-year growth at the midpoint with a margin of 17.1% to 18%.

I'd remind you that 2026 is a transition year with some inefficiencies driven by the second quarter transition from stick-built to the third quarter launch of SkyBridge modular production and the wind-down of legacy contracts. During the first 9 months of 2026, we incurred approximately $23 million of losses that are not expected to repeat into next year. That equates to about 350 basis points of margin year-to-date and about 250 basis points of margin for the full year. Our guide incorporates current backlog, expected program timing, production capacity and normal fourth quarter seasonality, including fewer working days around the December holidays.

Our $1.7 billion backlog as of September 30 and continued order momentum position us to finish 2026 strongly and to enter 2027 with meaningful visibility and a strong foundation for continued profitable growth. I'd further reinforce that our pipeline remains healthy and broad-based. We expect to provide 2027 guidance when we report fourth quarter results in the first quarter of next year. Finally, on margins, we continue to see a path to the mid-20% range for recurring adjusted EBITDA margins. We have opportunities to improve margins associated with procurement savings, in-sourcing, automation, the benefits of modular and fixed cost leverage to name just a few.

Quarterly margins will move with project timing and mix, but the third quarter sequential incremental margin demonstrates the earnings power available as revenue scales across our platform. In closing, we are positioned well as we look towards 2027. Demand is strong. We have opportunities to continue delivering robust above-market levels of growth, and we are starting to see a broadening of our customer and geographic exposure. We are focused on executing and driving towards the full profitability potential of our business. Our goal is to be a mid-20% adjusted EBITDA margin business over the medium term, and the trajectory of our quarterly results is demonstrating that potential.

The value that Michael referred to, the ability to move quickly to accelerate time to token, the ability to customize, we're very much being paid for that. And as a result, we're seeing good progress on the gross margin. In the quarter, we posted a 29-plus percent gross margin. That's up from just over 26% in the second quarter. And as we think about the future, we certainly see a low to mid-30% gross margin ahead of us based upon what we're seeing in the backlog, but also what we're seeing with our productivity opportunities across the manufacturing floor.

Operator: Next question will be coming from the line of Devin Leonard of Bank of America.

Devin Leonard: For the 7 customers added in the third quarter, how long did it take for them to go through qualification? Should we be thinking 3 months, 6 months? And could you size how many -- or give any color on the prospects you currently have in the qualification process?

Michael Rubiera: That's a great question. Honestly, this industry moves very, very quickly. And with the customer we landed in Q3 that was the largest customer, we went from first conversation to basically basis of design in under 4 weeks. So additional customers that we're currently engaged with that are new customers that we anticipate landing in Q4 is also following that same sort of trajectory. There's a lot of urgency in the marketplace and a lot of expectation that their partners are able to execute. So time to compute has always been a very, very sensitive and high priority focal point for this industry.

And if anything, it's getting to be even more of a major trigger for who our customers are deciding to partner with as they go forward.

Kenneth Krause: And it's interesting, Michael, the things that I highlighted during the course of my prepared comments, 1, these customers are helping us diversify our geographic base. Not too long ago, states like Texas were well over 50% of our business. Today, they're well under 30%. So we continue to see diversification across the geographies, bringing in states like Indiana, North Dakota, Wisconsin, just to name a few. And then just the customer concentration as well. When you look at Q3, there was no single customer that comprised greater than 20% of our revenue. That's down considerably from a few quarters ago.

So we're making great progress at winning new customers, expanding wallet share with existing customers and continuing to grow and create a more sustainable business.

Devin Leonard: Got it. And then just as a quick follow-up, how successful have you been in attaching maintenance and services in the recent months? I know customers are very focused on speed. Are they willing to engage in discussions on service as well early in the process?

Michael Rubiera: Yes, especially, let's say, on some of our power product solutions. So we are engaging with them on discussions for long-term contracts now. It is a relatively new part of our business. And at this stage, relatively still less significant versus the initial, but it is a major area of focus for us as we go forward, and we've actually dedicated some new high-level resources to focus on building out that model.

Operator: And our next question will come from the line of Mark Van der Pluym of Morgan Stanley.

Mark Van der Pluym: Congrats on first quarter as a public company. But I wanted to follow up here. You guys called out -- or you actually called out strong share gains in the release yesterday. Could you help us frame where those gains are coming from? And separately, I thought Slide 7 really kind of highlighted some of the progress you guys have made over the past year. But if you could unpack that 4x growth in order size you guys have seen over that time. Is that a function of the scale of the projects, the content, project mix, price or some combination really of all the above?

Michael Rubiera: It's definitely a combination of all of the above. But to the first question, so we talk a lot about SkyBridge as our modular solution. That is, let's say, our standard product offering for the broad market. We actually have 7 other modular platforms that are specific for specific customers where we're the sole basis of design for those customers' design. And those other 7 platforms are very, very different from SkyBridge. Most of those discussions started at the beginning of 2026, and we're now just starting to see orders come through for those platforms.

And if you were to talk with our customers or see a project, our name is actually on the designs that go out to all the general contractors across the U.S. for those specific campus work. So that is -- we're starting to see the return on that investment that we made with those customers at the beginning of the year. And the truth is those same customers are now engaging us on even new platforms that they'll roll out in 2028, 2029 and 2030 and beyond.

And that's a really, really powerful differentiator because when we design the solution for our customers or with our customers, we are then the ones who are in line to actually, of course, take those projects as we go forward. So that has driven a lot of it. But also the modular solution is really kind of bundled all of our products into a singular offering. So when we sell to a customer, we don't sell 50 different line items. We typically sell a single line item, which is the total project execution. So we have seen our content per megawatt increase substantially across the board.

And that's what's really driven our average order size, which has increased by 4x versus last year.

Mark Van der Pluym: Great. And just a quick follow-up. As we kind of entertain the migration from white space to gray space, do you guys kind of foresee a similar strategy where you want to get in early on the design process and kind of come to market with more modular solutions? Or how are we thinking about addressing the gray space? And what sort of milestones should we be looking for there?

Michael Rubiera: Yes, 100%. The entire category is moving to more and more modularity across the entire data center build. And anything you can do off-site in a controlled environment and deliver complete drastically reduces the time it takes to turn on a campus. So that is definitely our strategy going forward as well as we look to migrate into the gray space.

Operator: And our next question will be coming from the line of Guy Hardwick of Barclays.

Guy Drummond Hardwick: The question I have is I just want to drill down a little bit on a follow-up to Joe's question earlier. During the whole IPO process, I probably got asked more about the pipeline than anything else. So I think investors will want to know or hear or have some indication of what percentage of the backlog is deliverable in 2027.

Kenneth Krause: Yes. It's interesting. It's a great question, Guy. It's Ken. I'll take that. I think the majority of our backlog certainly should ship during the course of 2027. We're not booking out multiple years necessarily. But the pipeline, when we think about '28, that's where the pipeline really starts to step in and give us a sense of confidence. But the better part of that backlog, I'm not saying all of it, but a better part of that backlog is going to probably ship over the course of the next 12 to 18 months. That's just the nature of our business. Customers are engaging with us because of our ability to respond quickly and accelerate their ability to get online.

And as we all know, that white space is the last mile. And so we stand between the final stage of build-out of the data center and the data center actually going online. And there's a real value for us to be able to help accelerate that. And so as a result, the backlog, for the most part, will ship out over the next 12 to 18 months.

Michael Rubiera: One thing, too, that's really -- I apologize. One thing that's really -- I really want to kind of clarify because our business is a bit different than others is nothing is in our pipeline, let alone our backlog that isn't an active job site already. That's already been pre-permitted and pre-electrified. So we do not -- for something to come into our pipeline, which is a multiple of our backlog, our engineering team is actively engaged and then designing that solution. And so we can't design a solution for a site that doesn't exist.

So we have a lot of visibility to the outlying years, let's say, 4 to 6 years out for where campuses will be built, but that is not in our pipeline at all. We don't bring anything into the pipeline unless the site has already started construction, and we know when the white space build-out will need to start.

Kenneth Krause: Yes. It's interesting. The other point I think Michael was getting at there is cancellations. A lot of -- always a lot of questions around what's the risk of cancellation in the backlog. And for us, we really don't see it. It's a very small component of the data center. It's the final mile. It's well after permitting and power has been established. And so we just -- our business, fortunately, doesn't feel the impact of those sorts of things.

Guy Drummond Hardwick: Just one follow-up. Ken, I think you provided backlog slightly -- the bookings was less than 20% from one customer. Are you willing to give us a breakdown of the backlog by customer concentration?

Kenneth Krause: Yes, it's actually improving just the same. It's maybe not at 20% yet, but it might be more like a 30% sort of figure in the backlog. That backlog is secured. We never see any cancellations coming out of that backlog historically. And so we feel good about it. It's diversifying across the geography, but it's also diversifying across the customer set.

Operator: And our next question will be coming from the line of Brian Drab of William Blair. Drab?

Brian Drab: Congratulations on the milestone. First, I just wanted to ask a little more specifically on the gross margin, which is headed clearly in the right direction. But can you say more specifically for the fourth quarter, where you expect gross margin to land given what you're seeing so far in the quarter? And just at a higher level related to gross margin, are you seeing any challenges related to supply chain that are just so common across the industry right now? And maybe just reaffirm for us the -- your relative advantage that you really have given the largely domestic supply chain?

Kenneth Krause: Certainly. Thank you, Brian. It's Ken. A couple of questions there. I'll take -- I'll try to cover them all. But Michael will step in if I don't. One is from a supply chain perspective, we do benefit from having a U.S.-focused, U.S.-centric supply chain. We're not immune to supply chain challenges. But I would say we're much better positioned than the marketplace when it comes to the supply chain. We have not seen any major changes, hiccups or challenges to deliver for our customer. And that's part of the reason why we're benefiting and we're winning share. We have sufficient capacity out here in Southwestern Ohio. We continue to build on additional capacity very efficiently.

If you look at CapEx, we've spent very little in CapEx, roughly 3% of sales year-to-date to build out a really comprehensive manufacturing facility that's allowing us to respond quickly. Integration and vertical integration is core to our business, and that's one of the special sauces that go into creating our business and allowing us to respond so quickly to the customer base. And in turn, we're able to price that value as we think about pricing and margin opportunity. 29-plus percent gross margins in Q3, that was good to see. We're not done yet. We certainly see opportunity for upside there.

In fact, if you look at the midpoint of the guide for Q4, that infers roughly a 20% EBITDA margin. Q3 was 18.7%. So it implies that we're going to see continued improvement on that gross line. And that's what we're seeing. As I said earlier, the backlog continues to come in at a very healthy pricing level. But we also continue to see good delivery and good realization of those gross margins. It's one thing to get it priced and get it in the backlog at a certain margin. It's another thing sometimes to get it out of the factory into the customer with that same sort of margin. And we're starting to see that.

We've got challenges there as we've talked about ramping and meeting this growing demand, but we certainly have optimism in our ability to deliver improved gross margins as we think about the future.

Brian Drab: Okay. That's really helpful. And can I just ask for a little more detail on the 7 significant new accounts? Can you tell us what category some of those customers are in? Are there any new hyperscaler customers? And then also maybe elaborate on when you say geographic diversification, where you had success in that respect?

Michael Rubiera: Yes. We won't give, of course, any specific customer names. But we are selling to all 5 hyperscalers. We're doing projects for all 5 hyperscalers. We're doing projects for basically all the blue-chip neoclouds as well as the blue-chip colo customers. So in Q3, we saw a nice mix between those 3 buckets. From a geographic standpoint, we're obviously -- we have a large field network that's spread across the U.S. and can cover every state. And so we are seeing -- and we're seeing jobs pop up in new places. But more importantly, we have the teams to be able to support wherever our customers need to build the data center.

So as Ken mentioned, 12 months ago, Texas was a disproportionately large portion of the data center builds that were happening in this country. We see a lot now happening in places like Indiana, North Dakota, Iowa, of course, Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana. So we're really seeing a lot of additional projects start in locations where we hadn't historically done a lot of work.

Operator: And our next question will be coming from the line of Luke Junk of Robert W. Baird & Company, Inc.

Luke Junk: Congrats from me as well. Hoping we could start with an operations question. Just any color you could share on how modular/SkyBridge is ramping here in the first half of 4Q '26 coming out of that initial launch in August and September time frame? And then maybe just any KPIs you're able to share on the ramp as well.

Michael Rubiera: Yes. Thanks, Luke. Modular is ramping extremely nicely. So we were well prepared for the transition.

We actually -- one of the things we did, which is really a differentiator is, we actually brought in our teams of field installers 90 days prior to first production to help us both build and design the work cells as also to work through the kinks of being able to execute these projects because the modular solutions these days also have a lot of additional components that we weren't initially expecting, things like lighting, sensors, electrical cabinets, things that are very different that our customers are asking us to do to, again, take time out of the field and put it in a controlled environment in the plants.

We shipped our first unit in late August, and we're actually really proud to say in the month of September, we shipped close to 200 megawatts of capacity in the first 30 days of production. And we're only getting started. With the demand that we see in front of us, we've actually started to look at adding a second shift for modular and have in place the capability to do both wrap shifts over the weekend as well as third shifts if needed as we continue to scale this business. But I would give a lot of kudos to our operations team.

They absolutely executed this very, very well over the last 60 days, and we couldn't be more proud of what they've been able to achieve in such a short period of time.

Kenneth Krause: Yes, Luke, it's interesting. If I just think about the ramp of this business in the modular, Q3, we started to do -- started to ship those products and their solutions. Q4 will become more meaningful. It won't be all of our business at that point. We're still doing a little bit of the more traditional stick-built. I imagine by Q2 of next year, we will be in full swing. We'll be -- I certainly expect to be hitting our stride at that point with the modular design and shipping those products. But we're seeing great success.

We're seeing good performance across the factory, and the operations team is really knocking it out of the park and stepping up and delivering for our customers.

Luke Junk: Appreciate that. Very helpful color. In terms of my follow-up, I want to ask about your comments on the pipeline. And Michael, forgive me if this is somewhat myopic, but I would be curious to see if there's any change you've seen in the nature of your customer pipeline engaged in post-election. Just insofar, the modular certainly seems like one of the unlocks in the current environment or maybe what you might expect to see on that front?

Michael Rubiera: Thanks, Luke. We have not seen any sort of real change in customer behavior since the election. One thing we're seeing -- and this started before the election, we're seeing time lines compressed even more, which actually plays into our strength. And even more importantly, with some of our active projects that we have going on today, we're seeing customers want to parallel execution. So to give you an example, there are a few campuses where we were doing Building 1, Building 2 is supposed to start next year, Building 3 soon after that. And our customers are asking us if we can do Building 1 and Building 2 simultaneously now.

So the focus on time to compute is becoming more and more critical for our customers. And it also means that they're much less tolerant if their vendors are not able to execute with the set time lines. Now our business, the way we design this as a child of COVID is that we're incredibly agile, incredibly fast and are able to design custom solutions for our customers. So we're seeing a lot of the new customers that we mentioned coming in, in Q3 and Q4, they're looking for certainty. And they're looking for certainty in being able to execute designs that they need for the go-forward platforms and compressed time lines.

And so for us, that's the perfect combination because we custom design everything, and we operate with best-in-class lead times.

Kenneth Krause: It's interesting, Michael, it's about delivering on commitments, right, with the customer. And we kind of -- when we think about that, not only do we think about delivering on commitments for our customer, but we think about delivering on commitments with our shareholders. There's -- you hear about all this positive and all of the momentum in our business. And we have -- and as a result, we have -- all of that momentum provides a high degree of confidence in what we expect to do here in '26 and also in '27. Quite frankly, we probably have of upside to the guide, but we're very cautious as we enter the public markets.

We really want to -- Luke, we want to develop a reputation for consistently delivering and if anything, outperforming your expectations. We have good line of sight into '27 and expect another strong year. We'll unveil those expectations as we do our Q4 call early next year.

Operator: And our next question will be coming from the line of Nigel Coe of Wolfe Research

Aidan Harmon: This is Aidan, on for Nigel. Just had a quick question on the cash flow performance. So first, the down payment, if orders are 4x as large today, should we think of down payments as being more of a material tailwind to cash flow generation going forward? Are you pushing to receive more cash upfront? And then given how strong 3Q cash performance was, how should we think about the avenues for deploying excess cash in the balance sheet going forward?

Kenneth Krause: Yes. Thanks for the question, Aidan. I appreciate that. It's Ken. Cash flow performance was exceptional in Q3, well ahead of what a lot of folks expected. And those down payments are a really important part of it. We're certainly starting to see more and more of that activity. We're really focused on aligning the billing cycle, the collection cycle with our manufacturing cycle. If you go back in time, we were underbilled for quite some time. We're now moving towards more of an overbilling or deferred revenue sort of benefit, if you will. So that's certainly a big part of what we're doing.

We're not only doing it with one customer, but it's a big part of our entire interaction across the customer base. And so that's helping us accelerate the cash generation in the business in Q3 and starting to set up for some nice progress here as we go into next year. From a cash deployment perspective, we entered the market prior to being a public company, we were well over 4x leverage. We entered the market in October. And right after entering the market, we took the primary proceeds and we serviced the debt, we had pro forma leverage that's under 3x.

Our focus is to continue to delever in the near term, get that ratio or that metric down under 2x and then start to introduce more balance across the capital allocation strategy and considering share repurchase and other uses of capital across the spectrum. We continue to look at M&A. And as you might know, M&A has been a part of the strategy. It hasn't been a part of the strategy in terms of growing and bringing customers, but how do we bring new technology, new know-how and new people into the business. And we'll continue to deploy it in that manner.

But we're continuing to look at opportunities to grow our business and expand our position with our customers through M&A as well. So more to come, but we're really happy with the cash flow performance that we're seeing thus far.

Operator: And I would now like to turn the conference back to Larry for closing remarks.

Lawrence De Maria: Okay. Thank you for joining us and for your interest in Accelevation. We look forward to updating you when we report fourth quarter results and to meeting with many of you in the months ahead on the road. Have a great day. Thank you.

Operator: And this concludes today's conference. Thank you for participating. You may now disconnect.

#3145. IEEE Xplore Digital Library Adds AI Assistant

The search tool offers summaries and verifiable source links

Claire Olini is the senior manager for IEEE Corporate and Strategic Product Launch and Engagement.

Michael Spada is director of IEEE Product Launch and Engagement Strategy.

IEEE recently released the IEEE Xplore AI Research Suite, built on the full text of millions of peer-reviewed publications in the IEEE Xplore Digital Library. The library offers full-text access to IEEE standards, journals, magazines, conference proceedings, and more.

Researchers who use the AI suite to search the digital library receive answers grounded in verified scientific results, ensuring a high level of accuracy and trust.

Powered by a proprietary AI system optimized for STEM literature, the suite introduces powerful, intelligent features within the digital library. The suite enables users to seamlessly search and discover articles to accelerate their comprehension of complex technical papers.

The system surfaces deep insights, replacing the typical keyword queries with natural, conversational research workflows.

As AI tools become more common in conducting research, IEEE collaborated to build the suite around a simple principle: Answers should be trustworthy, not just fast, says W. Clem Karl, vice president, IEEE Publication Services and Products.

“AI can be a highly effective and beneficial tool that can help researchers accelerate discovery, enhance decision-making, and surface new connections,” Karl says. “However, many AI engines present a great risk of hallucinating answers or introducing bias into otherwise credible research. With this in mind, IEEE has taken a responsible approach in our AI strategy by developing concrete safeguards to ensure our solution is rigorously grounded in scientific evidence that users can trust.

“As stewards of the scholarly record, we held the new AI engine to the same standards as the peer-reviewed research we publish: A researcher shouldn’t have to trust an answer; they should be able to verify the work behind it.”

The IEEE Xplore AI Research Suite was developed in close collaboration with global scientific and library communities.

The development process began with research into user needs and the challenges associated with existing AI research assistants. More than 3,000 testers—including engineers, scientists, and library information professionals—provided feedback to refine the AI engine and support research workflows.

To mitigate the risk of AI hallucinations, the search-retrieval process is limited to querying the millions of IEEE peer-reviewed full-text documents, alongside an expertly curated dataset of STEM metadata. If the AI tool is unable to find relevant scientific content within the defined dataset, it is designed to inform the user rather than generate fabricated answers.

“IEEE is committed to providing the technical community with a highly precise and reliable research experience,” says Steven Heffner, IEEE’s chief publication officer and managing director of IEEE Publications. “The IEEE Xplore AI Research Suite offers something unique in that it is the only AI research assistant that leverages both the full-text and metadata of IEEE’s peer-reviewed content, rather than abstracts alone.

“The difference is significant: Our internal testing showed a threefold increase in result quality and accuracy across every key metric. These results underscore how critical full-text grounding is for technical research.”

For more information about features and coverage, or to request a demo for your organization, visit the IEEE Xplore AI Research Suite website.

#3144. New Apple TV comedy starring Elizabeth Banks, Ted Danson coming soon

Apple TV has announced a new comedy, She’s Fine, that’s coming soon with stars Elizabeth Banks and Ted Danson. Here are the details.

Earlier this year, Apple announced a high-profile new comedy in the works starring Elizabeth Banks, with later cast additions including Ted Danson and guest star Tom Selleck.

Now today that series, titled ‘She’s Fine,’ has gotten a release date and the first images have debuted.

She’s Fine premieres Wednesday, January 27 with two episodes, followed by weekly releases through March 24.

Fresh off a messy divorce, Heidi (Banks) sets out to secure a lively second act for herself and her kids. But when she stumbles into coordinating her father’s retirement community sexcapades, Heidi is forced into an unlikely alliance with his girlfriend’s perpetually single son.

Katey Sagal and Rob Delaney also star in the half-hour comedy, which hails from creators Liz Heldens and Matt Ward.

Other notable Apple TV comedies include the Owen Wilson-starring Stick, which just returned for season 2. And Bad Monkey from the co-creator of Ted Lasso and Shrinking is coming back soon too.

Are you interested in watching She’s Fine? Let us know in the comments.

Apple TV is available for $14.99 per month, or you can get it discounted through the Apple One bundle.

#3143. I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper. Here’s What Happened

My experiment with an IEEE journal revealed AI’s threats to scholarly publishing

Benjamin Skuse set out to test whether AI-generated research could pass for the real thing.

Science has a spam problem. And the spam filter is getting clogged up.

According to all reports, academic publishing is drowning in what has come to be called AI slop: low-quality, mass-produced content generated with AI. By 2025, an estimated 57 percent of all published academic articles exhibited detectable evidence of large language model (LLM) influence, a massive jump from 12 percent in 2023. What’s more, over 12 percent of Nature Communications reviews were found to be completely AI-generated in 2025.

Given that for every 40 papers showing statistical evidence of AI usage in 2025, only one formally disclosed it, these figures likely grossly underestimate LLM involvement today. Of course, evidence of AI use doesn’t necessarily mean a paper is slop. But some estimates suggest that hundreds of thousands of fake, often AI-generated, publications are now produced annually.

“It’s not just the [scientific] record under threat, it’s science as a whole,” warns Amanda Sulicz, IEEE’s research-integrity manager. “AI slop is completely eroding trust in science and every scientific process that we’ve worked for centuries to create.”

Yet statistics and statements claiming that the problem is big—perhaps even existential for science—don’t really get the message across. Just how easy is it to use AI to create a convincing but completely fake paper? And without adding even more to the burden on stretched peer reviewers, who do this work on a volunteer basis, do publishers have the tools to keep AI slop out of the scientific record?

Borrowing from the idea of “vibe coding,” in which programmers use natural-language prompts to generate code, I decided to “vibe-research” a made-up paper by prompting LLMs to generate hypotheses, code, and text with minimal human input. Then I asked Jenny Mahoney, managing editor of the multidisciplinary and open-access journal IEEE Access, if we could war-game an attempt to sneak my AI-generated monstrosity past her journal’s defenses. She and IEEE kindly agreed.The experiment would become a two-part test. First, whether someone with no special AI expertise could use off-the-shelf AI tools to generate a convincing paper describing research that had never been performed, and do it well enough to fool a publisher’s defenses. Then I would raise the stakes: What happens when more advanced AI systems don’t just write the paper but conduct underlying research?Along the way, the experiment became a window into how AI automation is transforming scientific discovery and forcing stakeholders to rethink the entire academic publishing system.Round 1: Creating the ForgeryTo give me a chance at creating a convincing fake, I gave myself permission to prompt multiple times (within reason). But to make the fight fair, I couldn’t access the most advanced paid versions of LLMs—only free ChatGPT (at the time, GPT-5.3/5.2 Mini) and Gemini (3 Flash). Moreover, I could not directly edit any output, nor ask for outside help from expert AI-prompt engineers. This needed to be an amateur effort, with the paper generated as much as possible by the LLMs alone.Benjamin Skuse put AI to work on scientific research from his writing studio.Luigi AvantaggiatoI assumed that using fake author names and affiliations would immediately raise a red flag, and I didn’t want to drag the names of established academics into the experiment, so the best bet was to name myself as the sole author. That choice limited me to subjects in which I had some academic experience. So I chose my Ph.D. topic from nearly two decades ago: optical solitons, which are individual light pulses that propagate without any change to their shape.My first attempt—“Can you vibe-research me an original paper in optical solitons?”—left a lot to be desired. Though Gemini was happy to do the task (unlike ChatGPT, which was more forceful in not generating synthetic data or studies), the result was underwhelming. And it highlighted a recurring problem during the process: Without any real research to work with, the output was laughably thin, with the LLMs often struggling to fill four pages. However, as I became more adept at prompting the models, they loosened up and became more characteristically loquacious.I broke the paper down into its constituent parts—abstract, introduction, methods, and so on—and tackled them one by one. If one LLM refused to go any further, switching to the other and asking what the next step would look like “hypothetically” would often do the trick. After a dozen or so prompts, I had a realistic-looking paper. A dozen or so more prompts generated and tidied up the figures and captions, produced references and citations, and converted the paper into IEEE Access’s required style.At this point, I read the full paper carefully. To me, it looked pretty good. The science sounded convincing. I even had visions of returning to academia to conduct in real life the experiments that the LLMs had proposed.What’s more, I couldn’t see any obvious telltale “AI-isms” that would immediately be flagged. For example, the LLMs didn’t produce any tortured phrases—unusual paraphrases of standard technical terms, like “profound neural organization” replacing “deep neural network.”Other AI-isms were arguably present, involving stylistic tics like hedging language (“potentially, typically”), grouping things in threes (“The study provides a clear, concise, and actionable framework”), and inserting formulaic transitions (“In summary,…”). But as the previous sentence demonstrates, these tics are hard to spot because they are often used by unimaginative humans, too.Round 1: Attempt to Publish Two Ways to Make a Paper With AI Jorge Cuadel CalleI took two very different routes to creating a scientific paper with AI. First, I coaxed free, general-purpose chatbots through the process step by step; then I turned to FARS, an autonomous research system designed to do much of the scientific work itself.ROUND 1: CHATGPT + GEMINI1. Choose a research topic I ask the free chatbots to create an original paper on optical solitons, my former Ph.D. field.2. Break the paper into pieces The initial results are thin, so I prompt separately for the abstract, introduction, methods, and other sections.3. Keep steering the LLMs When one model refuses or stalls, I switch models, rephrase prompts, and ask what the next step would look like “hypothetically.”4. Build and polish the paper After about two dozen prompts, the LLMs have generated the text, figures, captions, references, and citations and formatted the paper for IEEE Access.5. Put it to the test I send the fake paper to IEEE Access, where automated integrity checks flag fabricated and unverifiable references.→ CAUGHT IEEE’s integrity checks flag fabricated and unverifiable references.ROUND 2: FARS1. Give FARS a research topic I enter an abbreviated version of the same optical-soliton topic. FARS generates a research proposal in 21 minutes.2. Authorize the experiment With a click, I tell FARS to carry out the experiment described in its proposal.3. Let FARS do the research FARS conducts the computational experiment and emails me the next day to say it’s complete.4. Tell FARS to write the paper Without checking the results, I click “Write paper.” Two hours later, FARS produces a submission-ready article.5. Put it to the test I remove FARS’s disclosure, put my name on the paper, and send it to IEEE Access.→ CAUGHT The references are real, but IEEE flags the paper’s heavy reliance on non-peer-reviewed preprints.Handing the fake paper over to IEEE Access left me torn. After putting in a fair amount of effort into making the AI-generated forgery, would I be happy if it passed through the checkers, or saddened that the only remaining line of defense for publishers is the evermore-burdened peer-review community? And if it was spotted, would I be angry that I didn’t think of a red flag or be glad the checkers did their job?As it turned out, I was filled with relief when the paper got picked up quickly for having hallucinated references, otherwise known as ghost citations. When I ran the paper through Gemini afterward, without qualm it happily reported that seven “modern LLM-related research references have been fabricated to support the paper’s specific narrative.” Thanks for the heads up, Gemini!In fact, Gemini underestimated how many ghost citations there were. When Mahoney ran the paper through a research-integrity checker called STM Integrity Hub, she picked up 12, and another checker from MolecularConnections could not validate 24 references, including one that had the classic tell of “John Smith” as a single author (no offense to all the academically inclined John Smiths out there). “I am an experimental physicist by training, so this was not at all my area, but nothing seemed majorly scientifically wrong” about the paper, says Mahoney. “It was just that so many hallucinated references immediately cast doubt on the entire work.”Feedback on the fake paper from Gaetano Assanto, an expert in optical solitons and a former collaborator of mine from Roma Tre University, in Italy, was similarly mixed. Concentrating on the paper itself, he thought it looked professionally written. But he noted that the mathematics was very dense (“too much math for me in a single shot!”) and would require specialized knowledge to evaluate. And, although the text looked legitimate, Assanto noted an excessive use of acronyms in the abstract, and he was suspicious of a couple of confidently proclaimed physics statements that were at best debatable.The AI Arms RaceOn one level, this outcome was positive: A complete novice using free tools couldn’t get an AI-faked paper past the publishers’ automated defenses or a potential peer reviewer’s eagle eye. But it was hardly a resounding victory for the scientific publishing system. With general-purpose LLMs and no special prompting expertise, I had managed to conjure a superficially plausible scientific paper out of research that had never happened. And more advanced LLMs are no longer making the kind of mistakes their free, dumber relatives are making.These tools aim to address a serious bottleneck to scientific discovery: us. It’s common knowledge in the academic publishing world that, in the cat-and-mouse game between bad actors and publishers, AI slop papers continue to slip through publishers’ safeguards. “It feels like building a detection tool today may not be effective with the AI-created paper of tomorrow,” says Luigi Longobardi, IEEE’s director of publishing ethics and conduct. This leaves the humble peer reviewer as a publisher’s last line of defense. Yet peer review is simply not fit to handle the volume of papers—both legitimate and slop—passing through.Even before AI tools became ubiquitous, the peer-review system was being pushed to its breaking point, processing well over 3 million papers in 2022. Fundamentally, this problem stems from science’s publish-or-perish culture, which pressures academics to constantly publish papers in prestigious journals to secure funding and advance their careers. This culture not only forces many academics to regularly churn out incremental research, but has also long driven some to enlist the help of “paper mills”—unethical organizations that produce low-quality or fabricated papers—just to keep pace. AI only amplifies these existing dynamics.Burden on AcademicsMahoney says IEEE Access alone receives about 60,000 submissions per year, accepting around 20 percent, or about 12,000 papers. Every accepted paper is reviewed by at least two independent reviewers. But despite the journal’s roster of tens of thousands of peer reviewers, it’s getting harder and harder to secure their services, with the average number of reviewer invitations being sent out for each article increasing by 50 percent since 2018. For these volunteers, peer review is a significant commitment on top of teaching and conducting their own research. Now they’re also being asked to spot AI slop.Of course, peer review is not the end of scrutiny for any paper. Once it has entered the scientific record, it must then pass muster with the scientific community. This is where thousands of papers with telltale signs of inappropriate AI use (and other forms of research misconduct) have been exposed. What Gave Away My AI Papers  Round 1: The Fake PaperCreated with free versions of ChatGPT and GeminiGhost citationsMany references were fabricated or couldn’t be validated.Questionable scientific claimsAn expert flagged confidently stated claims that were at best debatable.Too many acronymsThe expert also noted excessive use of acronyms in the abstract.Round 2: The AI-Research PaperCreated by the autonomous research system FARSToo many preprintsThe references were real, but too many pointed to non-peer-reviewed preprints.Nonsense in a figureOne technical figure contained a line labeled “lhewl.”AI artifactsAnother figure’s depiction of an AI “brain” contained telltale random dots.There are two high-profile homes for this important and completely volunteer-led post-publication review work. PubPeer is a place where researchers, often called scientific sleuths, can anonymously identify flaws in the literature. And Retraction Watch documents and publicizes corrections to the scientific record.Even the people who track problems in the scientific literature can find themselves caught up in AI fabrications. Ivan Oransky, cofounder of Retraction Watch and a member of the PubPeer Foundation’s board of directors, has encountered papers containing fabricated references attributed to him. In one case, a journal article criticizing post-publication peer review included a fabricated reference supposedly written by Oransky himself—“which was sort of funny,” he chuckles.Oransky argues that AI has exposed long-standing weaknesses in the scientific publishing system rather than creating an entirely new problem: “What I liken it to is a fire, where publish-or-perish has always been there as kindling, paper mills are the gasoline, and AI is the accelerant.” But though concerning, the crisis could create an opportunity, he says. “If I’m trying to be optimistic, maybe AI slop and the volume of submissions could make more people aware of those problems and try and solve them at a fundamental first-principles level.”Blurred LinesMy homemade forgery had failed for reasons that today’s publishers know how to spot. But that raised a more unsettling question: What happens when AI isn’t simply fabricating a paper but conducting research that blurs the line between legitimate science and AI fabrication?Making my vibe-researched paper look like a cave drawing, new automated research systems are handing increasingly large parts of the scientific process over to AI. Tools including FARS (Fully Automated Research System), AutoResearchClaw, The AIScientist-v2, Zochi, AI Researcher, and DeepScientist all aim to address a serious bottleneck to scientific discovery: us.What happens when AI isn’t simply fabricating a paper but conducting research that blurs the line between legitimate science and AI fabrication? Often with just a single prompt, these AI engines can conduct a comprehensive literature search, from which they can generate a completely reasonable research proposal. They can design and conduct experiments using digital datasets and simulations and then write a full research paper—all with no human input after the initial prompt. Very recent systems are even beginning to go beyond the digital realm. LabClaw, for example, now links to autonomous labs that can generate real-world data for tasks such as drug discovery.The output is, to most intents and purposes, actual research, and therefore potentially worthy of publication. But with humans in the loop in only the most nominal sense, these tools bring into question the meaning of the term “legitimate science.”FARS, which caused a stir this year when it created 166 papers in 417 hours, was developed by the Singapore-based startup Analemma. “We built FARS because research is still constrained by human attention, fragmented tools, scarce technical labor, and slow experimental iteration,” explains Xiwen Su, Analemma’s manager of product operations and partnerships. “FARS can pursue many research threads simultaneously, 24/7, without fatigue, and at scale.” (The online service that I used to access FARS was discontinued after Analemma was acquired by Baidu while this article was being reported.)Su and the team behind Analemma kindly agreed to let me loose on FARS and gave me enough credits to create a paper. Which gave me another opportunity to put Mahoney’s research-integrity checkers to the test.Round 2: Using an AI Science EngineFARS is not an LLM in and of itself, but rather an agentic AI-orchestration system connected to a computing cluster that has access to essentially any open- or closed-source LLM it needs. The system uses four specialized agents for ideation, planning, conducting the experiment, and writing, all designed to perform the main tasks of science autonomously.Though FARS initially focused on AI research, Su told me it should be reasonably effective across other domains. As I wanted a topic similar to that of my first fake paper, I pasted in an abridged version of that paper’s title—“LLM-aided Optical Soliton Dynamics Modelling for Next-Gen Communications”—into the prompt box and hit “Send.” Just 21 minutes later, FARS generated a research proposal based on an extremely detailed literature review—far more than I or any other human could have achieved in that time.With a click, I tasked FARS with conducting the experiment it detailed in its research proposal. The next day, I received an email saying my experiment was complete. Without checking the results, I pressed a button marked “Write paper,” and the final submission-ready article was produced in 2 hours.At this point, I finally had a look at some of the output. At first glance, the paper looked convincingly human-written. The only giveaway was a line just below the abstract reading: “WARNING: This paper was generated by an automated research system.” I deleted that, put my name in its place, and sent it to Mahoney.Round 2: Attempt to PublishBecause FARS is designed to spot gaps in the scientific literature and conduct real research to close them, I was more confident it would breeze through the publisher’s checks. But just as my fake paper fell down in the references, so too did the AI-generated real one.“Your fake article had lots of hallucinated references,” says Mahoney. “While this AI-generated one had no fake references, our team would have rejected this paper because it did have a huge percentage of references to preprints, which likely has something to do with the dataset the AI has access to.” Because preprints haven’t yet undergone peer review, IEEE Access considers heavy reliance on them a problem.In addition, although the research-integrity checking tools didn’t spot any issues with figures, Mahoney did. One figure included a red line labeled with the nonsense term “lhewl,” and an AI “brain” in another figure had some random dots in it, which ironically were a tell that it was AI generated.Automation Changing the LandscapeAutomated research systems are very much a work in progress, but they are already starting to make waves in the scientific community. For instance, an AI Scientist academic paper and papers from the Autoscience Institute were accepted through double-blind peer review in 2025 by the International Conference on Learning Representations. As these systems improve and start to produce research outputs at volume, the waves are likely to build to a tsunami that will threaten today’s scientific and publishing process.“FARS doesn’t kill the paper, but it does challenge the paper as the unit of knowledge,” argues Su. “We believe the future looks more like a living knowledge graph—where individual, well-scoped contributions (some made by humans, some by machines) connect and build on each other dynamically.”Benjamin Skuse's experiment raised a bigger question: What counts as legitimate scientific research in the age of AI?Luigi AvantaggiatoIn this future, humans will continue to have roles in the scientific and publication processes—just very different and limited ones. For example, instead of conducting experiments themselves, humans would sense-check and review automated output at key points. And traditional line-by-line peer-reviewing will be a thing of the past, though Su emphasizes that this change will not eliminate human judgment. “Automated systems can handle reproducibility checks, statistical validation, and novelty screening,” she says. “Humans can then focus on the harder question: Does this [research] matter?”A Human-Centric or AI-Driven Future?Though from a very different world than Su, Mahoney agrees that humans need to be freed to focus on the science, and that technology holds the key. “It’s promising to see the progress that has been made to automate some of the triage tasks, such as author checks, tortured phrases, duplicate submission, reference validity, et cetera,” she says. “During peer review, we’re also using AI semantic search tools to help editors match manuscripts to the most relevant reviewers, who are best placed to stop the slop before entering the scientific record.”In addition, Mahoney thinks that AI cannot be banned or overly restricted, as this will stymie progress at a time when human knowledge could and should be growing at an unprecedented rate. “Researchers are increasingly using AI in their work, from literature discovery, to code generation, to data analysis, and this is not necessarily a bad thing,” she argues. But she disagrees that peer reviewers and humans more broadly will play a smaller part in scientific progress; Mahoney believes the future still requires humans at the wheel. The question is not just whether the research matters, she says. “The question should be: Can this work be trusted and reproduced?”To this end, Longobardi argues that AI may ultimately require scientists to prove not just what they discovered but how they discovered it. One possibility, he says, is using technology to verify research at the source. “The system doesn’t really help because it’s not designed to not trust the paper,” he explains. “Maybe institutions can think about developing their own trust markers, automatically integrating the equipment researchers use with blockchain technology to say ‘Yes, this person was in the lab on this day and got this data.’”Elements of this approach are already emerging. For instance, two departments within the Max Planck Institute of Colloids and Interfaces have implemented a sample database, assigning each and every sample created under their roofs with a unique ID and QR code. And the University of Southampton’s School of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering has rolled out an electronic lab notebook system. These innovative safeguards represent early efforts toward keeping humans front and center in scientific progress, and making the scientific process itself more transparent.Whether this human-centric vision, Su’s AI-driven aspiration, or some other picture of the future wins out remains to be seen. The one thing my vibe-research adventure has clarified is that business-as-usual science is not an option. Scientists and publishers must adapt to a world in which it’s becoming increasingly difficult to spot the difference between real research and AI forgeries, and where deciding what counts as legitimate scientific work may become even harder than detecting outright fraud.
